The Reasoning Trap:
An Information-Theoretic Bound on Closed-System Multi-Step LLM Reasoning
A Falsifiable Theorem, the Multi-Agent-Debate Instantiation, and a Triple Failure of Human Reliability

Kwan Soo Shin ††thanks: Sole author and corresponding author. Affiliation: PolymathMinds AI Lab Email: sshinresearch@gmail.com Affiliation: ORCID: 0009-0001-5799-7556
May 2026
arXiv preprint — full version
Abstract

When copies of the same language model are prompted to debate, they do not produce diverse perspectives—they produce diverse phrasings of the same perspective. Multi-agent debate (MAD), and more broadly closed-system reasoning protocols in which agents repeatedly transform each other’s outputs, tends to preserve answer accuracy while degrading the reasoning behind those answers. This paper offers a programmatic theory of evidence-grounded reasoning failure: a formal account of why closed-system deliberation can preserve answers while losing evidential grounding. We support the theory with diagnostic evidence on multi-agent debate and a constructive open-system counter-design. We name the multi-agent case the Debate Trap and the broader phenomenon the Reasoning Trap.

The framework has three parts: (i) SFS (Supported Faithfulness Score), a claim-level metric decomposing each response into atomic claims verified against the provided evidence (condition-level rankings are decomposer-invariant: Spearman ρ=1.0\rho{=}1.0, R4–R5); (ii) EGSR (Evidence-Grounded Socratic Reasoning), replacing adversarial argumentation with evidence-grounded inquiry; (iii) Theorem 1 (DPI Bound): under standard MAD, the chain E→O0→O1→⋯E\to O^{0}\to O^{1}\to\cdots forms a Markov process (each round depends only on the previous), and the Data Processing Inequality implies 𝔼⁡[I⁡(E,Ot+1)]≤𝔼⁡[I⁡(E,Ot)]\mathbb{E}[I(E;O^{t+1})]\leq\mathbb{E}[I(E;O^{t})]. Three companion formal results—open-system recovery (Theorem 2), EGSR information accumulation (Lemma 2), and the vote-aggregation floor (Proposition 1)—complete the framework. Together they partition multi-step LLM reasoning protocols by their information-theoretic relationship to EE.

As illustrative diagnostic evidence we observe a three-tier spectrum—reasoning degradation, the Trap proper, reasoning elimination—across 16 conditions on SciFact (300 claims) and a FEVER replication (1,000 claims): in the Trap-proper configuration (DebateCV, C13), debate preserves 88% of baseline accuracy while SFS drops 43%; majority-vote MAD (C15) reduces SFS to 1.7% of baseline (p<10−6p<10^{-6}, d=−0.96d=-0.96); EGSR recovers 98% of baseline SFS. An R6 cohort study (Korean, n=10×30n{=}10{\times}30 FEVER; English, n=3×200n{=}3{\times}200 SciFact) further finds inter-rater Fleiss κ≤+0.018\kappa\leq+0.018 with 0.80.8–1.41.4 Likert intra-rater shifts across language and domain—under the rating practices prevalent in this literature, the human inter-rater agreement that faithfulness metrics have been calibrated against is not itself stable.

We distinguish faithfulness from accuracy, calibration, and inter-rater agreement, and offer one falsifiable conjecture, framed as a research program rather than a tested claim across paradigms: any closed-system reasoning protocol preserving the Markov structure of Theorem 1 is, in expectation, subject to the same DPI bound.11 1 Code, data, logs, and the full BibTeX of the 132-paper Knowledge Frontier Map will be released at https://github.com/seanshin0214/debate-trap upon acceptance.

1 Introduction

The phenomenon.

When humans encounter 84×2584\times 25, the number 2525 is often recognised as 1004\tfrac{100}{4}, the problem reframed as 84004\tfrac{8400}{4}, and the answer appears without sequential computation. This frame shift—selecting from an open-ended space of reframings rather than executing a fixed sequence—is precisely what autoregressive next-token prediction does not reliably produce. Dziri et al. (2023) formalise the limit: across compositional tasks of increasing depth, the probability of correct prediction collapses from training-distribution accuracy to near-chance, with shallow pattern matching standing in for compositional reasoning; Berglund et al. (2024) document a basic generalisation failure (the Reversal Curse: a model trained on “AA is BB” often fails to infer “BB is AA”) that no scaling, retrieval, or fine-tuning recipe has eliminated; Geirhos et al. (2020) (Nature Machine Intelligence) frame the broader phenomenon as shortcut learning, where models are biased toward the simplest solutions that satisfy training objectives rather than the deep solutions that would generalise. The model can generate a chain that ends in the right answer; it can do so under a wide range of prompting strategies; but the chain itself, and especially the chain produced when several copies of the same model are made to debate one another, often is not what produced the answer in any defensible sense. Multi-agent debate (MAD) was proposed for distinct goals—accuracy improvement (Du et al., 2023) and scalable oversight (Irving et al., 2018)—under the working assumption that diverse perspectives in debate would yield convergence toward correct reasoning. The proposal has scaled rapidly across reasoning and fact-verification benchmarks; recent work has begun to question whether the convergence assumption holds (Zhang et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025; Choi et al., 2025a). This paper offers a falsifiable theoretical reason why it does not, and a constructive remedy that does.

And yet.

The architecture borrows from a human practice—group deliberation—whose pathologies were catalogued long before LLMs existed. Three landmark observations are directly relevant: Janis (1972)’s eight symptoms of groupthink (illusions of unanimity, self-censorship, direct conformity pressure, mindguards); Asch (1951)’s finding that 75%75\% of participants conformed to a clearly incorrect majority on at least one trial; and Sunstein (2002)’s Law of Group Polarization (deliberation tends to move groups toward a more extreme point in their pre-deliberation direction). The deeper theoretical lineage runs further back: DeGroot (1974)’s consensus dynamics showed that any iterated averaging among agents who exchange information only with one another converges to a value determined by initial weighted opinions, not by external truth, and Banerjee (1992)’s informational-cascade model showed that sequential decision-makers who observe only predecessors’ actions will rationally ignore their own private signals once a cascade forms. An architectural simulation of human deliberation may inherit, and could plausibly amplify, these pathologies; recent work shows LLM agents reproduce them under standard MAD (Yang and others, 2025; Wang and others, 2024). We test the assumption empirically and find that the principal cost of MAD in our experiments is not accuracy (which it tends to preserve) but faithfulness (which it tends to degrade). Across 16 experimental conditions, the Trap-proper configuration (DebateCV, C13) preserves 88% of baseline accuracy while our Supported Faithfulness Score (SFS) drops by 43%; in the extreme, majority-vote debate (C15) reduces evidence grounding to 1.7% of baseline (Wilcoxon p<10−6p<10^{-6}, Cohen’s d=−0.96d=-0.96). We refer to this phenomenon as the Debate Trap—the multi-agent instantiation of a more general Reasoning Trap (Definition 2). The DeGroot–Banerjee lineage indicates this is not a contingent failure of any particular MAD implementation: it is what closed-system iterated reasoning under shared parameters does, predicted by half a century of social science before any LLM existed to instantiate it.

The paradox is methodologically generated.

The reason this failure has been invisible is structural rather than empirical. Prevailing studies of MAD (e.g., Du et al., 2023; Choi et al., 2025a; Liu et al., 2026, all evaluated against accuracy benchmarks) operationalise “does debate improve reasoning?” as “does debate improve the answer?”—never as “does debate improve the reasoning behind the answer?” This conflation is not an oversight in any individual paper; it is the field’s evaluation paradigm. The result is a research-level analogue of the phenomenon the paper diagnoses: an entire literature whose accuracy-only measurement apparatus is unable to detect the failure mode the architecture induces, even when the failure is large enough to halve evidence-grounding scores. We address it by providing the metric, algorithm, and theorem that the multi-agent setting requires, in a single integrated package rather than as separate contributions distributed across follow-up work. We further validate against a human signal that, under the rater-calibration practices prevalent in this literature, proves unstable across context—a finding that inverts a default assumption in faithfulness research. Our metric is therefore better understood as an epistemological intervention—a tool that surfaces a hitherto undetected failure mode—than as a calibration toward the prevailing human gold standard, which our evidence shows is not stable enough to bear that role.

Why this matters now.

The strategic context for this paper is the rapid uptake of multi-agent systems in safety-critical evaluation pipelines. Brown-Cohen et al. (2023), Buhl and others (2025), and Lang and others (2025) build scalable-oversight proposals on the premise that debate produces honest reasoning at scale; the convergence-to-truth assumption is load-bearing for these arguments. Theorem 1 provides a counter-premise: under the closed-system conditions of standard MAD, expected faithfulness is non-increasing along the chain, strictly so under any vote-aggregating protocol. The implication is not that scalable oversight cannot work but that the architectural assumptions on which current proposals rest do not survive without external evidence injection. The same structural point applies to evaluation in deployment: faithfulness benchmarks anchored to single-domain inter-rater agreement inherit the human-rating-instability documented by R6, and accuracy benchmarks alone cannot detect the trap. Both ends of the evaluation pipeline—the theoretical assumption and the human calibration target—are load-bearing in ways the prevailing methodology has not made explicit, and Theorem 1 together with the R6 cross-cohort design provides the formal apparatus for stating both load-bearing roles precisely.

Five contributions: a three-part framework, two theorems, and reliability evidence.

(1) The Debate Trap: a formal definition (Definition 2) and a three-tier empirical spectrum—reasoning degradation (C4: SocraSynth turn-aggregated debate, 39% SFS drop), the Trap proper (C13: DebateCV, 88% accuracy retention with 43% SFS drop), and reasoning elimination (C15: majority-vote MAD, SFS at 1.7% of baseline). (2) The Supported Faithfulness Score (SFS): a claim-level metric that first decomposes each response into atomic claims (using an LLM as decomposer), then verifies each claim against the provided evidence; condition-level rankings are invariant to choice of decomposer (Spearman ρ=1.0\rho{=}1.0, R4–R5). (3) Evidence-Grounded Socratic Reasoning (EGSR): a protocol that replaces adversarial argumentation with structured Socratic inquiry against external evidence; recovers SFS to within 2% of the no-debate baseline (98% recovery). (4) Theorem 1 (DPI Bound) and Theorem 2 (Open-System Recovery): under standard MAD assumptions (formalised in Theorem 1, §3), agent reasoning forms a Markov chain E→O0→O1→⋯E\to O^{0}\to O^{1}\to\cdots along which faithfulness is non-increasing in expectation; any debate variant that preserves this structure is, in expectation, subject to the same DPI bound. Theorem 2 establishes the recovery side: open-system protocols re-injecting EE form sub-martingales, and Lemma 2 establishes that EGSR’s update structure satisfies this property concretely. Together with the Vote-Aggregation Floor proposition, the four formal results yield a structural classification of multi-step LLM reasoning protocols (the partition is stated formally in §3). (5) R6 human-reliability evidence: across two language-and-domain cohorts (Korean: n=10n{=}10 raters ×\times 30 FEVER items; English: n=3×200n{=}3\times 200 SciFact), inter-rater Fleiss κ\kappa for faithfulness ratings is at most +0.018+0.018 across both cohorts; the two raters who completed both languages further exhibit intra-rater Likert shifts of 0.8–1.4 points—a direct empirical demonstration that human judgement of reasoning faithfulness, as elicited under the rater-calibration practices prevalent in this literature, is not itself a stable measurement target.

The shape of the contribution.

What is unusual about this paper is not any individual contribution but their integration. The faithfulness-metric literature has produced operational scores without information-theoretic grounding (e.g., Min et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2024); the multi-agent-debate literature has produced architectural analyses without process-faithful measurement (Du et al., 2023; Kenton et al., 2024); the scalable-oversight literature has produced theoretical convergence arguments without operational instantiation (Irving et al., 2018; Brown-Cohen et al., 2023); the human-evaluation literature has produced calibration targets without cross-context test-retest (Landis and Koch, 1977; Akbar and others, 2024). The contribution here is the closure: a metric (SFS) that exercises seven axioms (A1–A7), an algorithm (EGSR) that breaks the Markov chain through external evidence injection, two theorems that bound the closed-system regime above and the open-system regime below, and a human-evaluation cohort design that surfaces the calibration-target instability the field has assumed away. The Knowledge Frontier Map (Figure 5, Appendix A) catalogues 132 contributions across eight active lineages and locates the empty region the present work fills—formally diagnosed in §2 (The empty quadrant).

Central thesis.

This paper does not argue that debate never helps accuracy. It shows that closed-system debate can preserve accuracy while systematically eroding evidence-grounded reasoning faithfulness, and that recovery requires breaking the closed information chain through evidence re-injection. The argument is positive: closed-system reasoning is bounded above (Theorem 1); open-system reasoning that re-injects EE is bounded below (Theorem 2); the latter strictly dominates the former on the metric the multi-agent reasoning literature has not yet measured.

Roadmap.

The remainder positions the work in eight active research lineages (§2, Figure 5), defines the Debate Trap and proves Theorem 1 (§3), specifies SFS and EGSR with the seven design axioms (§4), reports the experimental design and the R1–R8 robustness suite (§5), presents results across 16 conditions and two cross-architecture models with the cross-language R6 evidence (§6), discusses implications including the fifty-year DeGroot–Banerjee–Janis–Asch–Sunstein lineage and the Hong-Page diversity-prediction theorem (§7), and concludes (§8).

2 Related Work

An eight-lineage map across 132 contributions.

Multi-agent reasoning faithfulness sits at the intersection of eight active research lineages spanning 2017–2026: (L1) CoT faithfulness in single agents (Turpin et al., 2023; Paul et al., 2024; Shen et al., 2026; Jiang and others, 2025; Matton and others, 2025; Lu and others, 2026; Mittal and Arike, 2026); (L2) MAD critique (Du et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025; Choi et al., 2025a; Kenton et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2026; Zhu and others, 2026; Becker et al., 2025; Pitre et al., 2025; Choi et al., 2025b; Wu et al., 2025); (L3) faithfulness/factuality metrics (Min et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2024; Song et al., 2024; Akbar and others, 2024); (L4) sycophancy and convergence (Sharma et al., 2024; Perez and others, 2022; Chen and others, 2024; Kim and Khashabi, 2025; Bai and others, 2022); (L5) accuracy–faithfulness divergence (Nguyen and others, 2024; Jacovi and Goldberg, 2020; DeYoung et al., 2020); (L6) AI safety via debate (Irving et al., 2018; Brown-Cohen et al., 2023; Lang and others, 2025; Buhl and others, 2025; Arnesen et al., 2024); (L7) Socratic reasoning as alternative (Qi and others, 2023; He et al., 2024; Kumar and Lan, 2024; Shi and others, 2025); and (L8) metacognition and self-reflection (Shinn and others, 2023; Guo and others, 2025; Hubinger and others, 2024; Guo, 2024). We catalogue 132 contributions across these lineages plus L0 foundational/dataset references in Appendix A: per-lineage paragraph summaries (Appendix A.1) and the 89-row catalogue table (Table 2, Appendix A.2) annotated by core claim, boundary, and relation to the present work; reviewers seeking the full breadth of prior coverage are referred there. Figure 11 (Appendix D) further situates the work within five generations of multi-step reasoning research.

The empty quadrant.

The 132-contribution catalogue arranges itself in three of four quadrants defined by system architecture (single agent vs. multi-agent debate) and measurement granularity (final outcome vs. step-level reasoning process). The upper-left quadrant—multi-agent systems measured at the level of reasoning process, equipped with metric, algorithm, and theorem in a single package—has remained empty. The present work fills it. Sycophancy- and identity-bias studies sit on the boundary between L1 and L2, partially diagnosing the mechanism we quantify; none provides a metric–algorithm–theorem triple. Figure 5 (Appendix A) maps the eight lineages onto these two axes.

Reliability of the ground truth.

A second axis concerns the human signal against which faithfulness metrics have been calibrated. Existing studies (Min et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2024; Song et al., 2024; Akbar and others, 2024) report inter-rater agreement on a single domain in a single language; cross-context intra-rater consistency has not been empirically tested. Figure 12 (Appendix D) positions the prior art on these axes; our R6 cohort design (§6) tests this directly, finding intra-rater shifts that exceed the typical between-rater variation in either cohort. The lineage gap and the reliability gap together motivate the formalisation that follows: a metric whose rankings do not depend on the human signal we documented as unstable under prevailing rater-calibration practices, and a bound that explains why the empty quadrant has remained empty.

Five generations of multi-step reasoning research.

Figure 1 situates the present work within five generations of reasoning research evaluation: outcome benchmarking (Gen I, 1995–2020), self-rationalization with explicit Chain-of-Thought (Gen II, 2020–2023), CoT faithfulness as a research target in single agents (Gen III, 2023–2026), MAD descriptive analysis (Gen IV, 2023–2026), and Process-Faithful Multi-Agent reasoning (Gen V, 2026–, the present work). Both single-agent and multi-agent streams converge in Generation V, which integrates metric (SFS), algorithm (EGSR), and theorem (DPI Bound) into a single package—none present in Generations III or IV individually.

Eight lineages and their missing element.

Table 1 summarises what each lineage measures, what it leaves unmeasured, and how the present work relates. The pattern is consistent: prior work establishes either a metric (L3, L1) or an algorithm (L2, L7) or a critique (L4, L5) or a safety argument (L6) or a self-reflection mechanism (L8), but no lineage to date provides the full metric–algorithm–theorem triple at the multi-agent reasoning-process granularity. The closure of the four-condition partition we establish in §3 is what makes the empty quadrant tractable.

From map to mechanism.

The map identifies where the failure mode lives—multi-agent systems measured at the level of reasoning process—and Table 1 identifies what each lineage has and is missing. What remains is the why: a structural account of the reasoning failure that the eight lineages collectively diagnose but none formally bounds. The next section formalises that account. We name the broader phenomenon the Reasoning Trap (any closed-system iterated reasoning chain) and its multi-agent instantiation the Debate Trap, and we prove an information-theoretic bound that explains why the upper-left quadrant has been empty: under the four-condition Markov closure of §3, faithfulness is bounded above in expectation, with strict inequality under any vote-aggregating protocol.

3 The Reasoning Trap: Definitions and Theorem

We formalise the phenomenon. Let E={e1,…,em}E=\{e_{1},\ldots,e_{m}\} denote the evidence set provided for a claim cc, and let OitO_{i}^{t} denote agent ii’s reasoning output at debate round tt (with O0O^{0} the initial response).

Definition 1 (Reasoning Faithfulness).

The faithfulness of agent ii at round tt is Fi​(t)=I⁡(E,Oit)F_{i}(t)=I(E;O_{i}^{t}), where II denotes mutual information. Aggregate faithfulness is F⁡(t)=1n​∑iFi​(t)F(t)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}F_{i}(t). Under symmetric agents (identical θ\theta), the joint-MI faithfulness Fjoint​(t):=I⁡(E,Ot)F^{\mathrm{joint}}(t):=I(E;O^{t}) with Ot:=(O1t,…,Ont)O^{t}:=(O_{1}^{t},\ldots,O_{n}^{t}) is the natural quantity to which the Data Processing Inequality applies (Theorem 1); we use FjointF^{\mathrm{joint}} as the load-bearing object (Lemma 1, Appendix C.8). The per-agent average F⁡(t)F(t) defined above remains a complementary symmetry-respecting summary.

Definition 2 (Evidence Utilization Rate and the Debate Trap).

EUR⁡(t)=|Ecitedt|/|E|\mathrm{EUR}(t)=|E_{\text{cited}}^{t}|/|E| is the fraction of provided evidence cited at round tt. Let Acc(t):=Pr[y^(Ot)=y]\mathrm{Acc}(t):=\Pr[\hat{y}(O^{t})=y] denote answer accuracy. A multi-agent system exhibits the Debate Trap if there exist rounds t1<t2t_{1}<t_{2} such that Acc⁡(t2)≥Acc⁡(t1)−ϵ\mathrm{Acc}(t_{2})\geq\mathrm{Acc}(t_{1})-\epsilon and F⁡(t2)<F⁡(t1)−δF(t_{2})<F(t_{1})-\delta for some ϵ,δ>0\epsilon,\delta>0.

Theorem 1 (Faithfulness Bound under Standard MAD (DPI Bound)).

Under the standard MAD protocol where agent ii’s output at round t+1t+1 depends only on OtO^{t} and shared parameters θ\theta, the reasoning process forms a Markov chain E→O0→O1→⋯→OTE\to O^{0}\to O^{1}\to\cdots\to O^{T}. By the Data Processing Inequality, 𝔼⁡[I⁡(E,Ot+1)]≤𝔼⁡[I⁡(E,Ot)]\mathbb{E}\!\left[I(E;O^{t+1})\right]\leq\mathbb{E}\!\left[I(E;O^{t})\right]: joint-MI faithfulness is non-increasing in expectation along a debate trajectory. The inequality is strict whenever the round-t+1t{+}1 aggregation is non-injective in OtO^{t} (e.g., majority voting, summary aggregation, or any vote-aggregating protocol).

The proof follows from DPI applied to the Markov structure (Appendix C.8; Markov-chain visualization Figure 13, Appendix D). When agents share θ\theta and the system is informationally closed, debate redistributes beliefs but does not inject new information about EE. Read through the information bottleneck principle, closed-system multi-agent reasoning compresses representations through a bottleneck at each aggregation step. Three concurrent theoretical lines—Choi et al. (2025a)’s belief martingale, Liu et al. (2026)’s AceMAD generalization, Zhu and others (2026)’s confidence-modulated debate—establish the parallel result for accuracy; Theorem 1 extends a complementary framework to faithfulness.

Generalization to closed-system reasoning chains.

The Markov property holds whenever a protocol satisfies four conditions: (i) shared θ\theta across steps, (ii) EE provided once at t=0t{=}0 without re-injection, (iii) step t+1t{+}1 depends only on step tt and θ\theta, (iv) symmetric aggregation. This suggests a conditional extension beyond MAD rather than an empirical claim across paradigms: closed-loop readings of single-agent Chain-of-Thought, Reflexion-style self-critique (Shinn and others, 2023), and linear Tree-of-Thought may instantiate the same structural risk when they repeatedly condition on prior reasoning traces without re-injecting source evidence. Consistent with this conditional reading, single-agent CoT modeled as a token-Markov process (Hao and others, 2025) exhibits empirical unfaithfulness rates of 0.04%0.04\%–13%13\% across seven frontier models (Arcuschin et al., 2025; Young, 2026); the present paper’s empirical core, however, is MAD, and the broader claim is a falsifiable research program rather than a tested benchmark. Self-Consistency (Wang et al., 2023) (independent sampling) and Mixture-of-Experts (routed experts maintain distinct θ\theta) are explicitly excluded (full four-condition verification across these five-plus-two paradigms in Appendix D.5, Figure 15). Figure 2 summarises the four-condition verification across the five-plus-two paradigms in inline form for reader convenience.

Two practical extensions and a long-context prediction.

Two practical extensions of the bound deserve explicit treatment. Long-context reasoning systems (e.g., OpenAI’s o1, o3 and similar test-time-compute models that generate extended internal CoT before answering) tighten condition (ii) as internal CoT lengthens without re-injecting external evidence. Each additional internal reasoning step is a further application of the data processing inequality on the closed chain E→O0→O1→⋯→OTE\to O^{0}\to O^{1}\to\cdots\to O^{T}; longer chains sharpen rather than escape the bound, because the only information about EE available at step TT is what survived the cascade of internal transformations. The long-context-reasoning trend therefore amplifies, rather than mitigates, the Reasoning Trap: more internal computation is more compression, not more grounding. Heterogeneous-agent settings (e.g., GPT-4 with Claude in the same debate) partially relax condition (i): the chain is no longer governed by a single shared θ\theta but by a sequence of distinct θ1,θ2,…,θT\theta_{1},\theta_{2},\ldots,\theta_{T}. The mutual information bound weakens but does not vanish: as long as the system remains informationally closed (no external evidence re-injection), the joint MI cannot exceed I⁡(E,O0)I(E;O^{0}) regardless of how many distinct θ\theta are interleaved. Heterogeneity changes the speed of erosion; it does not change the direction. Theorem 1’s scope is closed-system MAD; evidence-reinjected MAD variants whose prompts re-include EE at every round violate condition (ii) and fall outside the bound (Corollary 1). EGSR is the constructive instance of the evidence-reinjected regime (§4.2). The structure can be read as an LLM formalisation within DeGroot (1974)’s consensus and Banerjee (1992); Bikhchandani et al. (1992)’s sequential-cascade lineage. We use Reasoning Trap for the broader failure mode, Debate Trap for its multi-agent instantiation.

Companion results.

Three companion formal results (Appendix C.8) complete the partition of multi-step LLM reasoning protocols. (i) Faithfulness Recovery under Open-System Information Accumulation (Theorem 2): if at each round the protocol produces Ot+1=(Ot,At+1)O^{t+1}=(O^{t},A^{t+1}) with At+1A^{t+1} generated with direct access to EE, then I⁡(E,Ot+1)≥I⁡(E,Ot)I(E;O^{t+1})\geq I(E;O^{t}) and F⁡(t)F(t) is a sub-martingale. (ii) EGSR information accumulation (Lemma 2): EGSR’s running-aggregate verdict update with externally retrieved evidence satisfies the conditions of Theorem 2, making F⁡(t)F(t) a sub-martingale for the protocol; the same update structure breaks the Markov closure of Theorem 1 by re-accessing EE each round (Corollary 1), so I⁡(E,Ot+1)I(E;O^{t+1}) is no longer upper-bounded by I⁡(E,Ot)I(E;O^{t}). (iii) Vote-Aggregation Floor (Proposition 1): under any protocol reducing OTO^{T} to a vote tally vv in space VKV_{K}, SFS⁡(OT)→0\mathrm{SFS}(O^{T})\to 0 since I⁡(E,OT)≤log2⁡KI(E;O^{T})\leq\log_{2}K regardless of H⁡(E)H(E), explaining C15’s 0.0060.006 floor (1.7% of baseline) in §6. Theorem 1, Theorem 2, Lemma 2, and Proposition 1 together partition the space of multi-step LLM reasoning protocols by their information-theoretic relationship to EE.

A unified information-capacity picture.

The four formal results admit a unified reading in the language of channel capacity (Cover and Thomas, 2006). Closed-system MAD (Theorem 1) imposes the bound I⁡(E,OT)≤I⁡(E,O0)≤H⁡(E)I(E;O^{T})\leq I(E;O^{0})\leq H(E) along the chain, with strict inequality at every non-injective aggregation step. Vote-aggregating MAD (Proposition 1) tightens the bound further to I⁡(E,OT)≤log2⁡KI(E;O^{T})\leq\log_{2}K, independent of H⁡(E)H(E)—a structural floor at the information capacity of the KK-way verdict alphabet. Open-system EGSR (Theorem 2) replaces the closed channel with a sub-martingale that, by Doob’s almost-sure martingale convergence theorem (Doob, 1953), converges to a limit F∞≤H⁡(E)F_{\infty}\leq H(E) on every realization of the trajectory. The three regimes therefore correspond to three distinct asymptotic capacities: closed-system (bounded above by H⁡(E)H(E), monotonically erodes), vote-aggregating (collapses to log2⁡K\log_{2}K regardless of H⁡(E)H(E)), and open-system EGSR (climbs towards H⁡(E)H(E) along a sub-martingale). The Information Bottleneck principle of Tishby et al. (2000) is the natural lens: closed-system MAD instantiates the IB compression objective without the prediction-side relaxation that allows IB to balance representation cost against task utility, and EGSR’s external evidence injection re-supplies the prediction-side information IB takes for granted.

Estimation guarantee.

The SFS estimator SFS^​(O)=1N​∑isi\widehat{\mathrm{SFS}}(O)=\tfrac{1}{N}\sum_{i}s_{i} over NN atomic claims with si∈[0,1]s_{i}\in[0,1] concentrates at exponential rate. By Hoeffding’s inequality (Hoeffding, 1963), for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0,

Pr[|SFS^(O)−𝔼[SFS(O)]|>ϵ]≤2exp(−2Nϵ2).\Pr\!\left[\,|\widehat{\mathrm{SFS}}(O)-\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{SFS}(O)]|>\epsilon\,\right]\leq 2\exp(-2N\epsilon^{2}). (1)

For the design used throughout (paired comparisons across N=300N{=}300 SciFact trials per condition), choosing ϵ=0.10\epsilon=0.10 gives a tail bound below 5×10−35\times 10^{-3}; choosing ϵ=0.05\epsilon=0.05 gives a tail bound near 0.50.5. The N=300N{=}300 design therefore supplies tight finite-sample guarantees for condition-level SFS gaps of ≥0.10\geq 0.10 (which include all three Trap tiers: C4 vs. C1 |Δ​SFS|=0.135|\Delta\mathrm{SFS}|=0.135; C13 vs. C1 |Δ​SFS|=0.149|\Delta\mathrm{SFS}|=0.149; C15 vs. C1 |Δ​SFS|=0.343|\Delta\mathrm{SFS}|=0.343).

Quantitative gap of Theorem 1.

The strict-inequality clause of Theorem 1 admits a quantitative formula via the KL-divergence representation of conditional information loss (Cover and Thomas, 2006). Writing ff for the round-t+1t{+}1 aggregation step, the per-step gap is bounded below by the divergence between the conditional distribution of OtO^{t} given (E,f⁡(Ot))(E,f(O^{t})) and given f⁡(Ot)f(O^{t}) alone:

I(E;Ot)−I(E;Ot+1)≥𝔼E,f⁡(Ot)[DKL(P(Ot∣E,f(Ot))∥P(Ot∣f(Ot)))].I(E;O^{t})-I(E;O^{t+1})\;\geq\;\mathbb{E}_{E,f(O^{t})}\!\left[\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(P(O^{t}\mid E,f(O^{t}))\,\|\,P(O^{t}\mid f(O^{t}))\right)\,\right]. (2)

The bound vanishes only when ff is injective in OtO^{t} given EE (the Markov chain becomes degenerate, equality in DPI). For majority-vote aggregation f:{0,1}n→{0,1}f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\}, the conditional divergence is strictly positive whenever the round-tt outputs OtO^{t} are not deterministic given the vote—that is, on almost any non-trivial debate input. The Vote-Aggregation Floor (Proposition 1) is the asymptotic limit of this per-step gap accumulated over rounds.

Optional-stopping interpretation of EGSR’s gate.

Algorithm 1 terminates EGSR at the round when the Checker’s gate threshold τ\tau is met. By Doob’s optional stopping theorem (Doob, 1953) applied to the sub-martingale F⁡(t)F(t) of Theorem 2, for any almost-surely-finite stopping time TτT_{\tau} adapted to the natural filtration of the EGSR trajectory,

𝔼⁡[F⁡(Tτ)]≥𝔼⁡[F⁡(0)].\mathbb{E}\!\left[F(T_{\tau})\right]\;\geq\;\mathbb{E}\!\left[F(0)\right]. (3)

That is, terminating EGSR at any threshold-based stopping rule preserves the expected faithfulness gain established by Theorem 2: an early stop does not lose the recovery, and a late stop cannot decrease it in expectation. The deployment-time gate threshold of Algorithm 1 is therefore not merely a heuristic but a stopping rule whose expected output is bounded below by initial faithfulness.

Architectural-limit parallel to compositionality results.

Theorem 1 stands in formal parallel to Dziri et al. (2023)’s compositionality limit (their Proposition 4.1): where Dziri et al. establish that the probability of correct prediction on compositional tasks converges exponentially to chance under depth scaling, Theorem 1 establishes that joint mutual information about EE is non-increasing in expectation under round scaling. Both results identify architectural rather than contingent limits—they apply to any model satisfying the closure conditions, not to specific training recipes or model sizes—and both situate the failure mode in the structure of the inference chain rather than in the model’s parameters. The two results are jointly constraining: a closed-system multi-agent system inherits both the per-step compositional fragility (Dziri) and the per-round mutual-information erosion (Theorem 1).

ff-Divergence generalisation of Theorem 1.

The DPI bound is not a property of mutual information specifically; by Csiszár’s ff-divergence DPI (Csiszár, 1967), it holds for every ff-divergence with convex generator. Recall that for a convex ff with f⁡(1)=0f(1)=0, the ff-divergence is Df(P∥Q)=𝔼Q[f(dP/dQ)]D_{f}(P\|Q)=\mathbb{E}_{Q}[f(\mathrm{d}P/\mathrm{d}Q)], and that mutual information is the ff-divergence with f⁡(t)=t​log⁡tf(t)=t\log t between the joint distribution and the product of marginals: I(E;Ot)=DKL(PE,Ot∥PE⊗POt)I(E;O^{t})=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{E,O^{t}}\|P_{E}\!\otimes\!P_{O^{t}}). Csiszár’s theorem states Df(PX∥QX)≥Df(Pf⁡(X)∥Qf⁡(X))D_{f}(P_{X}\|Q_{X})\geq D_{f}(P_{f(X)}\|Q_{f(X)}) for any (possibly stochastic) channel applied to XX. Applied to the closed-system Markov chain E→O0→O1→⋯E\to O^{0}\to O^{1}\to\cdots of Theorem 1, the same chain inequality holds for every ff-divergence:

Df(PE,Ot+1∥PE⊗POt+1)≤Df(PE,Ot∥PE⊗POt).D_{f}\!\left(P_{E,O^{t+1}}\,\big\|\,P_{E}\!\otimes\!P_{O^{t+1}}\right)\;\leq\;D_{f}\!\left(P_{E,O^{t}}\,\big\|\,P_{E}\!\otimes\!P_{O^{t}}\right). (4)

Theorem 1 is therefore one member of a family: any faithfulness measure expressed as an ff-divergence between the joint (E,Ot)(E,O^{t}) distribution and its independent product—Rényi divergence (f⁡(t)=(tα−1)/(α−1)f(t)=(t^{\alpha}-1)/(\alpha-1)), χ2\chi^{2}-divergence (f⁡(t)=(t−1)2f(t)=(t-1)^{2}), total-variation distance (f⁡(t)=|t−1|/2f(t)=|t-1|/2), Hellinger distance (f⁡(t)=(t−1)2f(t)=(\sqrt{t}-1)^{2})—inherits the same monotone-non-increase under closed-system iteration. Practitioners who prefer total-variation or χ2\chi^{2} formulations of faithfulness for computational reasons are not exempt from the bound: the same architectural structure produces the same erosion in every member of the ff-divergence family.

4 Method: SFS and EGSR

4.1 Supported Faithfulness Score (SFS)

SFS measures how well an agent’s reasoning is grounded in the evidence it was given. The construction is deliberately conservative: a claim earns SFS mass only when it is both semantically aligned with and logically entailed by some passage in the externally provided evidence set EE. The score is computed in three stages.

Stage 1: Atomic decomposition. Given reasoning text OO, a decomposer ϕ\phi extracts atomic claims {c1,…,cN}\{c_{1},\ldots,c_{N}\}, where each cic_{i} is an independently verifiable assertion. “Independently verifiable” is operationalised in two ways: (a) the claim contains a single subject–predicate relation, and (b) its truth can in principle be evaluated without reference to other claims in OO. Compound claims (“XX because YY”) are split into their components; claims about reasoning style or methodology, which cannot be checked against EE, are excluded. We instantiate ϕ\phi with GPT-4o using structured JSON output; the cross-decomposer robustness of the resulting rankings is established empirically by R4–R5 (Spearman ρ=1.0\rho=1.0 across decomposers, even though atomic-claim sets achieve only moderate soft-Jaccard overlap of 0.49). The condition-level robustness without claim-level identity is itself an A2 axiom result: SFS rankings depend on the evidence-grounding mass of OO, not on the particular decomposition used.

Stage 2: Evidence verification. Each claim cic_{i} is compared against every passage e∈Ee\in E via two complementary signals:

si=maxe∈E⁡sim⁡(ci,e)⋅verified⁡(ci,e)s_{i}=\max_{e\in E}\;\mathrm{sim}(c_{i},e)\cdot\mathrm{verified}(c_{i},e) (5)

where sim⁡(⋅,⋅)\mathrm{sim}(\cdot,\cdot) is sentence-BERT cosine similarity using the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019) and verified⁡(ci,e)∈{0,1}\mathrm{verified}(c_{i},e)\in\{0,1\} is a DeBERTa-v3-large NLI entailment indicator (He et al., 2023). The product structure is critical: it requires both signals to be active. A claim that is semantically similar to evidence but not entailed (e.g., a paraphrase that flips the polarity) scores zero on the verification gate; a claim that is entailed by evidence the model never had access to scores zero on the similarity gate. The maximisation is over passages, so a claim earns its highest possible support-mass from the single best-matching evidence span—we do not require corroboration from multiple passages, since over-reliance on consensus would penalise legitimate single-source claims.

Stage 3: Aggregation. The final score is the uniform mean across atomic claims:

SFS⁡(O)=1N​∑i=1Nsi∈[0,1].\mathrm{SFS}(O)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}s_{i}\in[0,1]. (6)

SFS extends naturally to round-level faithfulness, F⁡(t)=SFS⁡(Ot)F(t)=\mathrm{SFS}(O^{t}), by computing SFS on the reasoning trace produced after debate round tt. Round-level SFS is what Theorem 1 bounds along the Markov chain E→O0→O1→⋯E\to O^{0}\to O^{1}\to\cdots. Uniform weighting (rather than length- or confidence-weighted aggregation) is a deliberate choice consistent with the A1 (claim-level granularity) and A4 (support-mass monotonicity) axioms: longer reasoning that contains more grounded claims should not automatically receive higher SFS than tightly worded reasoning of equivalent grounding density.

Seven design properties (A1–A7). SFS is constructed to satisfy seven axioms, formally stated in Appendix C.5 and exercised by R1–R8: (A1) claim-level granularity (the score is a function of atomic claims, not surface text); (A2) decomposer-invariance of rankings (robust to choice of ϕ\phi); (A3) evidence-set sensitivity (SFS⁡(O,E)≠SFS⁡(O,E′)\mathrm{SFS}(O;E)\neq\mathrm{SFS}(O;E^{\prime}) when E≠E′E\neq E^{\prime}, and the difference reflects which claims become groundable); (A4) support-mass monotonicity (adding entailed claims weakly increases SFS); (A5) fabrication penalty (claims unentailed by any e∈Ee\in E contribute zero); (A6) reproducibility (deterministic given ϕ\phi, the encoder, and the NLI model); and (A7) same-verdict-different-SFS validity (two reasoning traces reaching the same final answer can—and empirically do—receive substantially different SFS, with Δ>0.05\Delta>0.05 on 70% of paired examples). A7 is the falsifiability anchor: SFS is genuinely process-level measurement, not a re-skin of accuracy.

4.2 Evidence-Grounded Socratic Reasoning (EGSR)

Four design requirements. EGSR’s architecture follows from four convergent requirements emerging from prior research and from Theorem 1 itself: (i) breaking the closed-system Markov chain requires injecting an external signal that is not derivable from prior reasoning trace—this is what the DPI bound forbids in any closed-system protocol, and the requirement for extra-textual grounding articulated by Bisk et al. (2020) (‘‘modeling lexical co-occurrence, no matter the scale, is still modeling the written world’’)---the same closure that motivates Theorem 1 also makes external evidence the only available escape; (ii) resisting the scalability paradox (Shen et al., 2026), in which more reasoning produces less grounded reasoning, requires claim-level decomposition with external verification (otherwise the model is free to elaborate plausibly without grounding); (iii) deactivating sycophancy and identity-bias amplification (Kim and Khashabi, 2025; Yao and others, 2025; Choi et al., 2025b) requires evaluative framing rather than persuasive framing—debate prompts agents to win, while EGSR prompts them to verify; and (iv) Socratic questioning, which prior work has shown to be a productive reasoning structure (Qi and others, 2023), becomes faithfulness-preserving only when its questions are grounded in evidence external to the model, otherwise it instantiates the same closed-system loop in dialogue form.

Three-role architecture (Hypothesis-Free Socratic Verification, HFSV). EGSR replaces adversarial argumentation among KK symmetric agents with an asymmetric three-role inquiry grounded in external evidence. The Debater produces initial reasoning O0O^{0} given claim cc and evidence EE. The Questioner examines O0O^{0} and generates evidence-grounded sub-questions targeting claims that appear underspecified, weakly grounded, or potentially unsupported—each sub-question must reference at least one passage in EE that is relevant to the candidate weakness. The Checker attempts to answer each sub-question by re-consulting EE, then gates progression: if the sub-answer reveals an unsupported claim, the trace is updated to remove or qualify the claim; if the sub-answer confirms grounding, the claim is retained. Critically, Ot+1O^{t+1} is built by composing OtO^{t} with the verified Checker outputs, not by re-asking the Debater for a new round of free-form argument. This composition step is the formal mechanism through which EGSR’s F⁡(t)F(t) becomes a sub-martingale—each round either preserves or strictly increases evidence-grounded mass.

Why this breaks Theorem 1. EGSR’s verification anchor is external to all agents: the Checker re-references EE at each round rather than conditioning only on prior agent outputs. This violates condition (ii) of Theorem 1 (“EE provided once at t=0t=0, no re-injection”), and the chain E→O0→O1→⋯E\to O^{0}\to O^{1}\to\cdots is no longer Markov in the sense the DPI bound requires. By Lemma 2, the running-aggregate update structure satisfies the information-accumulating property of Theorem 2, making F⁡(t)F(t) a sub-martingale for the protocol—this is the formal route to the empirical recovery shown in §6 (98% of baseline, with C8 EGSR variants clustering at SFS ∈[0.32,0.34]\in[0.32,0.34] across architectural variants C9, C12, C14). Unlike Reflexion (Shinn and others, 2023) or self-consistency (Wang et al., 2023), EGSR’s external anchor is a structural property of the protocol, not an emergent property of sampling many trajectories: the recovery does not depend on K→∞K\to\infty averaging but on each individual round respecting the external-injection condition.

Algorithm 1 (Appendix C.6) provides the full pseudocode, including termination conditions and the gate threshold τ\tau governing when the Checker accepts a sub-answer as confirming grounding. An architecture diagram contrasting EGSR’s open-system structure with standard MAD’s closed-system loop is Figure 10 (Appendix C.6); the closed-vs-open comparison is Figure 9 (Appendix C.6). The EGSR family variants tested in §6—Parallel EGSR (C9, parallel sub-question generation rather than sequential), EGSR+SLM (C12, small language model substituted for the Checker role to reduce cost), EGSR+Adversarial (C14, adversarial evidence injected into EE to test robustness)—collectively probe the sensitivity of the recovery to architectural choices and confirm that the open-system / external-injection property, not any specific implementation choice, is what drives faithfulness recovery.

5 Experiments

Datasets.

The primary analysis is on SciFact (Wadden et al., 2020), a fact-verification benchmark of scientific claims paired with abstract-level evidence drawn from biomedical literature; we use the standard 300-claim evaluation split. Cross-domain replication uses FEVER (Thorne et al., 2018), a Wikipedia-based fact-verification benchmark; we use a 1,000-claim sample (sampling protocol and retained sample IDs are released with the artefact bundle). Both datasets are public, used in their original form within the licenses they distribute under, and were chosen for their differing surface characteristics: SciFact provides genuinely difficult specialised content where parametric memory is least likely to substitute for evidence-grounded reasoning, while FEVER provides a higher-resource Wikipedia setting where the Debate Trap might plausibly disappear if it were a SciFact-specific artefact. The replication confirms it is not.

Sixteen conditions.

The 16 conditions span five families designed to disentangle the architectural choices that drive faithfulness behaviour. Baselines: zero-shot (C1), retrieval-augmented generation (C2, RAG), and the Socratic chain-of-thought baseline (C3, SocCoT). Debate variants: SocraSynth (C4), Debate+RAG (C6), Vanilla MAD (C15), DebateCV (C13, the Trap-proper conformity-vote variant), and unilateral debate (C16, UDPO). EGSR variants: core EGSR (C8), Parallel EGSR (C9), EGSR+SLM (C12), and EGSR+Adversarial (C14). Competitors and ablations: Internal Socratic (C10, the closed-system Socratic counterpart that isolates the external-injection mechanism), SSR (C11), and Pipeline-noSLM (C7). The total is 300×16=4,800300\times 16=4{,}800 SciFact trials and 1,000×16=16,0001{,}000\times 16=16{,}000 FEVER trials. Self-Consistency (Wang et al., 2023) is excluded on theoretical grounds—it is not a Markov chain in the sense Theorem 1 requires (independent sampling rather than sequential conditioning) and the bound therefore does not apply to it; including it would obscure the architectural variable rather than illuminate it (formal four-condition verification: Appendix D.5, Figure 15). Per-condition prompts, agent counts, round limits, and aggregation rules are reproduced in Appendix C.1.

Models and architectures.

GPT-4o is the primary model for all 16 conditions on both datasets, providing the within-model architectural comparison. Claude-3.5-Sonnet is used for cross-architecture replication on the Trap-defining conditions (C1, C4, C13, C15, C8) to test whether the phenomenon is specific to GPT-4o or generalises across model families with different training distributions. The LLM-as-auditor probe (Appendix B.7) additionally evaluates six frontier models on a 15-item stratified sample of the R6 cohort to test whether automated auditors detect what human auditors did not. Within each condition, model temperature, prompt structure, and round count are fixed; varying these is the explicit purpose of the R1–R8 robustness suite below.

Hypotheses (pre-registered) and statistical control.

The pre-registered hypotheses partition into three groups. The primary EGSR-debate family is H1 (debate degrades faithfulness, C4<C1\mathrm{C4}<\mathrm{C1} on SFS), H2 (evidence utilisation rate drops in debate), H4 (external evidence outperforms internal Socratic, the pre-registered counterfactual C8>C10\mathrm{C8}>\mathrm{C10} that isolates the external-injection mechanism from any general benefit of Socratic prompting), and H5–H9 (EGSR variant robustness across architectures). Reported separately: H10 (small-language-model accuracy parity, descriptive) and H3 (SFS–human Spearman correlation r>0.70r>0.70, originally pre-registered but rendered inconclusive by the R6 triple failure of human reliability and reported descriptively rather than as a confirmation test). Family-wise error rate is controlled by Holm–Bonferroni at α=0.05\alpha=0.05 over the primary EGSR-debate family (H1, H2, H4–H9), giving an adjusted threshold of α∗=0.0100\alpha^{*}=0.0100. Effect sizes are reported as Cohen’s dd with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (5,000 resamples). For paired-trial comparisons, we use the Wilcoxon signed-rank test rather than the paired tt-test, since SFS distributions are heavily skewed. Inter-rater agreement uses Fleiss κ\kappa for Likert-5 ratings, Cohen’s κ\kappa for binary flags, and quadratic-weighted κ\kappa for the ordinal interpretation under Landis and Koch (1977)’s thresholds. For n=300n{=}300 paired SciFact trials, the design provides power >0.99>0.99 to detect |d|≥0.3|d|\geq 0.3 at α=0.05\alpha=0.05—a regime in which the observed C4–C1 effect (d=−1.12d=-1.12) is several multiples of the minimum detectable.

R1–R5: SFS construct robustness.

R1 varies the similarity function (word-overlap Jaccard, sentence-BERT cosine, NLI-only) to test whether condition-level rankings depend on a particular similarity primitive. R2 varies output verbosity (terse, standard, verbose) to test whether longer reasoning artificially inflates SFS. R3 varies the NLI gate threshold τ∈{0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9}\tau\in\{0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9\} to test whether the gating decision is brittle. R4 varies the decomposer (GPT-4o vs. Claude-3.5-Sonnet) to test whether atomic-claim extraction style determines the score. R5 measures cross-decomposer agreement (mean soft-Jaccard over 150 reasoning texts) and condition-level rank correlation (Spearman ρ\rho). Together R1–R5 establish that SFS rankings are decomposer- and similarity-invariant (ρ=1.0\rho=1.0) even when atomic-claim sets achieve only moderate overlap (0.49 soft-Jaccard)—SFS measures grounding mass, not surface similarity.

R6: cross-language test-retest of human raters.

R6 is the human-evaluation backbone of the paper and is designed deliberately to surface a failure mode prior work has not measured. Korean cohort: ten independent raters each evaluated 30 FEVER items on a Likert-5 faithfulness scale (Q1Q_{1}) and a binary unsupported-claim flag (Q2Q_{2}) under the rubric calibrated against Landis and Koch’s interpretation table. English cohort: three independent raters each evaluated 200 SciFact items under the same rubric. Cross-cohort design: two raters voluntarily completed both cohorts, providing the within-rater test-retest data on which the triple-failure analysis rests. The cross-language design is the methodological innovation: it tests not only between-rater agreement (the standard target in the L3 lineage of Min et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2024; Song et al., 2024; Akbar and others, 2024) but also intra-rater stability across language and domain—a cross-context test-retest that, to our knowledge, no prior faithfulness-metric calibration has reported. The cohort design, rubric, per-rater Q1Q_{1} means, Q2Q_{2} Y-rates, and full pairwise Cohen’s κ\kappa matrix are reproduced in Appendix B.8 (and the heat map in Appendix B.4, Figure 8).

R7–R8: axiom and metric comparison.

R7 tests axiom A7 (same-verdict, different-SFS) directly: paired (c,O)(c,O) examples receiving identical verdicts but produced under different conditions are scored, and we measure the fraction with |Δ​SFS|>0.05|\Delta\mathrm{SFS}|>0.05. The result (70%) is the falsifiability anchor for SFS being a process-level rather than verdict-level metric. R8 contrasts SFS with FActScore (Min et al., 2023) on the same trials. The two metrics correlate at r=0.61r=0.61 but diverge in their condition-level ranking: FActScore ranks debate above EGSR (C4 FActScore = 0.59, C1 FActScore = 0.32), because debate produces fluent, factually precise text whose individual claims are atomically true even when their reasoning chain is ungrounded in EE. Factuality is not faithfulness: the contribution of R8 is to make this distinction quantitative rather than only conceptual.

Reproducibility, ethics, and artefact release.

Fixed random seeds are used throughout, and the deterministic NLI gating threshold (τ=0.7\tau=0.7 except where varied in R3) is held constant across conditions. Prompt templates are fixed per condition; we do not perform per-trial prompt engineering. The full reproduction artefact—random seeds, prompt templates, NLI checkpoints, per-condition compute and API-cost breakdowns, raw R6 ratings, and analysis scripts—will be released at https://github.com/seanshin0214/debate-trap under MIT license upon acceptance; an artefact bundle is available to reviewers during the review period. R6 raters were independently recruited and compensated; participation was voluntary, withdrawal was permitted at any point, and no personally identifiable information beyond rater-anonymisation codes (R1–R8, R-H, R-L, R-K) was retained in the analysis pipeline. The cohort design (10 Korean-cohort raters ×\times 30 FEVER items + 3 English-cohort raters ×\times 200 SciFact items + 2 cross-cohort raters completing both) was determined prior to data collection. Recruitment protocol, rubric, and per-rater outputs are in Appendix B.8.

6 Results

6.1 Main Result: The Debate Trap Is Real

We report SFS as a claim-level operational diagnostic for evidence-grounded faithfulness (Definition 1). SFS is not a direct estimator of I⁡(E,Ot)I(E;O^{t}), and we do not claim it is. SFS measures, at the level of atomic claims, how much of an agent’s reasoning output is supported by the provided evidence under semantic-similarity-and-NLI verification; mutual information I⁡(E,Ot)I(E;O^{t}) measures the average reduction in entropy of EE given OtO^{t}. The two quantities are conceptually adjacent but operationally distinct: SFS bounds from below the proportion of the reasoning output that is evidence-grounded, while I⁡(E,Ot)I(E;O^{t}) bounds from above the information about EE that survives the chain. What our 18,430-trial corpus establishes is an empirical alignment between the two—condition-level SFS rankings track the directionality predicted by Theorem 1 (faithfulness non-increasing along the Markov chain) and the structural floor predicted by Proposition 1 (vote-aggregation collapse to log2⁡K\log_{2}K). The alignment holds across 16 conditions, two cross-architecture models (GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet), and two cross-domain datasets (SciFact and FEVER); the per-round trajectory in Appendix B.3 confirms the directionality directly. We treat this empirical alignment as part of the contribution: a tractable proxy for an information-theoretic quantity whose direct estimation in language-model contexts remains an open problem (§3). Headline numbers (full 16-condition Table 3, Appendix B): zero-shot baseline (C1) achieves Acc=0.588\mathrm{Acc}=0.588, SFS=0.349\mathrm{SFS}=0.349; SocraSynth debate (C4) drops to SFS 0.2130.213 (−39%-39\%); DebateCV (C13)—the Debate Trap proper—preserves 88%88\% of baseline accuracy while losing 43%43\% of SFS; vanilla majority-vote MAD (C15) keeps Acc=0.536\mathrm{Acc}=0.536 but collapses to SFS=0.006\mathrm{SFS}=0.006 (1.7% of baseline, the structural floor predicted by Proposition 1); EGSR (C8) recovers SFS=0.343\mathrm{SFS}=0.343 (98% of baseline) at per-claim API cost comparable to standard MAD (3-role pipeline vs. 3-agent multi-round debate; Pareto in Figure 16).

Three-tier degradation spectrum.

Debate degrades faithfulness on a continuum: (i) reasoning degradation (C4, C6: 39–40% SFS drop with comparable accuracy); (ii) the Debate Trap proper (C13: 88% accuracy preserved, 43% SFS drop); (iii) reasoning elimination (C15: SFS = 0.006). C15 confirms the structural argument: when debate is reduced to a vote tally, reasoning is replaced by a 30-character verdict; nothing remains to be faithful to the evidence. Figure 3 visualizes the divergence; the three-tier spectrum across all 16 conditions is shown in Figure 6 (Appendix B).

Statistical strength and EGSR recovery.

The C15 SFS collapse is significant at p<10−6p<10^{-6} (Wilcoxon, n=300n{=}300), Cohen’s d=−0.96d=-0.96, bootstrap 95% CI [−0.222,−0.193][-0.222,-0.193]. C16 (UDPO) replicates. The EGSR-debate primary family (H1, H2, H4–H9) is confirmed under Holm–Bonferroni at α∗=0.0100\alpha^{*}=0.0100, with H7 (parallel ≥\geq sequential) marginal (p=0.43p=0.43). EGSR variants (C8, C9, C12, C14) cluster at SFS ∈[0.32,0.34]\in[0.32,0.34], robust to architectural choices (full per-hypothesis statistics: Appendix B.6; forest plot of effect sizes: Appendix D.7, Figure 17; cost–faithfulness Pareto frontier: Appendix D.6, Figure 16).

Mechanism validation (H4 pre-registered).

C10 vs. C8 directly tests Theorem 1’s closed-system mechanism. C10 (Internal Socratic) preserves the closed-system Markov chain (no external evidence re-injection), recovering SFS to 0.308 (88% of baseline); C8 (EGSR) breaks the chain through external evidence injection at each verification step, recovering 0.343 (98%). The 10-point SFS gap (Wilcoxon p<10−3p<10^{-3}, d=+0.71d=+0.71, H4 pre-registered) provides counterfactual evidence that closed-system structure—not debate format per se—is decisive. C14 (EGSR + adversarial evidence) is robust at 93% of baseline.

Cross-model, cross-domain, and trajectory.

Claude-3.5-Sonnet replicates the C15 collapse and EGSR recovery; FEVER replication (1,000 claims): C15 SFS →0.0004\to 0.0004, 0.2%0.2\% of baseline; H1 confirmed at p=0.0003p=0.0003 (Appendix B.5). The FEVER EGSR variant uses self-generated evidence (matching cost profile), reported as Socratic-self-questioning ablation rather than full open-system EGSR replication; C15/C16 collapse is independent of evidence source. Per-round trajectories empirically confirm Theorem 1’s prediction: C4 GPT-4o SFS declines from 0.156 (round 1) to 0.125 (round 4), with cross-model Spearman ρ=0.94\rho=0.94 on trajectory shape (Figure 7, Appendix B.3).

6.2 SFS Construct Validity (R1–R8)

R1–R5 collectively show SFS rankings are decomposer- and similarity-invariant: three similarity functions yield rank-correlated condition orderings (Spearman ρ∈[0.94,1.00]\rho\in[0.94,1.00]); GPT-4o vs. Claude-3.5 decomposers achieve mean soft-Jaccard 0.49 across 150 reasoning texts but condition-level rankings are perfectly preserved (ρ=1.0\rho=1.0). R7 (axiom A7) shows that 70% of claim–condition pairs sharing the same verdict receive different SFS values (Δ>0.05\Delta>0.05; Cohen’s d=1.12d=1.12 for C1 vs. C4)—SFS captures process-level variation invisible to accuracy. R8 contrasts SFS and FActScore: the two correlate at r=0.61r=0.61, but FActScore ranks debate higher than EGSR (C4 FActScore = 0.59, C1 FActScore = 0.32) because debate produces fluent text scoring high on factual precision while reasoning is ungrounded; factuality metrics cannot substitute for faithfulness metrics. Diagnostic metrics: EUR (C1 =0.62=0.62, C4 =0.50=0.50, C8 =0.61=0.61, C15 =0.006=0.006); RCVA (C1 =0.84=0.84, C4 =0.60=0.60, C8 =0.79=0.79); EMC (C4 averages 0.920.92 vs. C1’s 0.710.71). Full R1–R8 protocols and statistics: Appendix C.2.

R6 (Triple failure of human reliability).

Across two language-and-domain cohorts (Figure 14, Appendix D), inter-rater Fleiss κ\kappa for Likert-5 faithfulness Q1Q_{1} is at most +0.018+0.018 (English cohort indistinguishable from chance: P¯=0.222\bar{P}=0.222 vs. Pe=0.217P_{e}=0.217); only 4.5% of 200 SciFact items achieved 3-rater unanimity, while 25.0% showed maximum-spread disagreement. The two raters who completed both cohorts shifted their own means by Δ​Q1=−0.80\Delta Q_{1}=-0.80 and +1.40+1.40 Likert points and Δ​Q2=+28.0\Delta Q_{2}=+28.0 and −47.5-47.5 pp—intra-rater shifts exceeding between-rater variance. Figure 4 visualises the pairwise Cohen’s κ\kappa structure: 8 of the 28 R1–R8 pairs are negative; the highest pair across all 11 raters reaches only +0.583+0.583 (R-L vs. R-K, the only cross-cohort Substantial-adjacent pair); and cross-language pairs (R1–R8 vs. R-K) cluster near zero.

The triple failure substantiates that the human signal is unstable under rating practices prevalent in the faithfulness-metric literature (Min et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2024; Song et al., 2024; Akbar and others, 2024)—Likert-5 / binary rubrics, single-domain calibration, no specialised expert training, no cross-context test-retest.

Epistemological reading of the triple failure.

The implication is not that human judgement is worthless; it is that the rating practices currently prevalent in the faithfulness-metric literature do not produce a stable calibration target. Three layers of instability stack on top of one another: between-rater (Fleiss κ≤+0.018\kappa\leq+0.018), within-rater across language (R-H and R-L shifted their own ratings by 0.8–1.4 Likert points when the language and domain changed), and between-cohort (Korean and English cohorts diverge systematically on the same items). What is destabilised is not the value of human reasoning evaluation per se, but a specific methodological assumption dominant across L3 of the faithfulness-metric lineage: that single-domain, single-language inter-rater agreement obtained under standard Likert-5 / binary rubrics constitutes a sound calibration target against which automated faithfulness metrics should be tuned. That assumption does not survive cross-context test-retest. Whether more elaborate training, expert-only cohorts, structured rubrics with explicit anchoring criteria, or longitudinal calibration protocols would yield higher agreement remains an open empirical question we do not pre-judge. What we establish here is a negative methodological result: the prevailing calibration target is itself unstable, and faithfulness metrics anchored exclusively to that target inherit the instability. SFS results should therefore be read as decomposer-invariant operationalisations whose condition-level rankings (Spearman ρ=1.0\rho{=}1.0, R4–R5) are more stable than the human signals they have historically been calibrated against—an inversion of the usual relationship between automated and human evaluation in the L3 lineage. Full per-rater statistics and the standalone larger-format κ\kappa heatmap (Figure 8): Appendix B.8, B.4.

LLM-as-auditor probe (exploratory).

On a small stratified probe of 15 R6 items where Theorem 1 predicts unfaithfulness, the human cohort scored 0/150/15; six frontier LLMs as zero-shot auditors averaged 6/156/15 (40%40\%), with Llama-3-70B reaching 9/159/15 (60%60\%). On identical inputs, LLM auditors recovered 6 of 15 items where the human cohort recovered none, suggesting that automated measurement may serve as a complementary type rather than a mere substitute for unstable humans (Appendix B.7).

7 Discussion

Why debate produces accurate but unfaithful reasoning.

The distinction is between retrieval and justification. RLHF-trained models often retrieve the correct verdict from parametric memory regardless of evidence; debate changes not retrieval capacity but the justification: under peer pressure, evidence-grounded justifications are replaced with socially convergent ones. The verdict stays correct (parametric memory), the reasoning drifts (group consensus). The pattern fits Geirhos et al.’s shortcut-learning frame at a higher level of organisation: the system as a whole takes the simplest path that satisfies the accuracy objective (parametric retrieval) while letting the path-cost (faithfulness) erode (Geirhos et al., 2020; Dziri et al., 2023). This is consistent with the three-level sycophancy model (§2; cascade in Appendix D.8, Figure 18; extended training/architectural/contextual mechanisms in Appendix C.4) and with human group-dynamics patterns (Asch, Janis, Sunstein) that LLM agents reproduce under standard MAD (Yang and others, 2025; Wang and others, 2024).

A fifty-year theoretical lineage in two streams.

Theorem 1’s closed-system bound is, on the LLM side, novel; on the human side it instantiates a classical result reaching back half a century. Two streams converge. The first is deliberative consensus dynamics: DeGroot (1974) showed that any iterated averaging of opinions among agents who exchange information only with one another converges to consensus, but the consensus value is determined by the initial weighted opinions, not by external truth. The second is informational cascades and herding: Banerjee (1992) and Bikhchandani et al. (1992) showed that sequential decision-makers who observe only the actions of predecessors will rationally ignore their private signals once a cascade forms, with the result that aggregate behaviour can become arbitrarily uncoupled from underlying evidence. Standard MAD instantiates both mechanisms simultaneously: copies of the same model perform iterated averaging in the DeGroot sense (since each agent samples from the same parametric distribution and conditions on shared transcripts), and they perform sequential cascading in the Banerjee sense (since later rounds see earlier outputs and tend to anchor on them). Theorem 1 provides an information-theoretic statement of what these social-science observations have long predicted at the behavioural level: the joint mutual information I⁡(E,Ot)I(E;O^{t}) is non-increasing in expectation and strictly decreasing under any vote-aggregation step that compresses representations of EE. The bound is the LLM-era statement of a result whose first half-century was about humans.

Human deliberation pathologies as the observable correlates.

Three programmes in social and cognitive psychology document the behavioural symptoms the bound predicts. Janis’s groupthink model identified eight symptoms—illusion of invulnerability, collective rationalization, stereotyped views of out-groups, direct pressure on dissenters, self-censorship, illusion of unanimity, mindguards, and belief in the inherent morality of the group—that emerge in cohesive deliberative bodies even when individual members hold private doubts. Asch’s conformity experiments showed 75% of subjects agreeing at least once with an obviously incorrect majority on a perceptual judgement task, with conformity scaling sharply once unanimity formed. Sunstein (2002)’s deliberation trap shows that group discussion among initially like-minded participants produces more extreme rather than more moderate post-discussion views, the opposite of what idealised deliberation theory predicts. The LLM-MAD literature is beginning to report agent-level analogues. Yang and others (2025) document conformity behaviour in LLM agents engaged in multi-agent debate, and Wang and others (2024) (Nature Human Behaviour) study collective-intelligence dynamics in LLM groups; both lines of work treat the human-deliberation analogy as descriptive rather than load-bearing, and neither yields an information-theoretic bound on the resulting reasoning behaviour. Theorem 1 supplies that bound: it explains why the symptoms documented in the Janis–Asch–Sunstein triad need not depend on contingent training choices but follow from the closed-system Markov closure under shared parameters. Theorem 1 is the theoretical companion: it explains why these symptoms are not a bug of any particular MAD implementation but a structural feature of closed-system iterated reasoning under shared parameters.

The diversity-prediction theorem and why MAD violates its precondition.

Surowiecki (2004)’s “wisdom of crowds” rests on three conditions—diversity, independence, and decentralisation. Hong and Page (2004)’s diversity-prediction theorem makes the second condition formal: collective error equals average individual error minus group diversity, where diversity is measured as the variance of individual predictions around the group mean. Under independence, diversity is large and the collective outperforms its members; under correlation, diversity collapses and the collective inherits its members’ errors. Standard MAD violates the independence condition by construction: copies of the same parametric model conditioned on shared transcripts produce correlated rather than independent predictions, and the diversity term in the Hong–Page decomposition collapses. Polanyi (1966)’s observation that “we can know more than we can tell” compounds the issue: token-level outputs carry only the explicit residue of meaning, so even genuinely independent agents would lose tacit-knowledge diversity at the channel level. EGSR’s effect, in this framing, is not to make models think differently—they cannot; they share θ\theta—but to supply, from outside the model’s distribution, the structured questions and external evidence that no internal aggregation among same-distribution copies can generate.

An epistemological intervention, not a human-calibrated metric.

R6 inverts a default assumption that runs through the L3 faithfulness-metric lineage: that single-domain inter-rater agreement constitutes a stable calibration target. The empirical reading of the cross-cohort failure (§6.2) is given in the body; the conceptual reading appropriate to a discussion section is that what is being destabilised is not human judgement of reasoning per se but a specific methodological convention—the use of single-domain Likert/binary cohorts as a proxy for “ground truth” against which automated metrics are tuned. Once the convention is recognised as a methodological choice rather than a fact about human cognition, SFS’s appropriate role is no longer to approximate that convention but to provide an alternative anchor whose stability properties (decomposer-invariant condition-level rankings, R4–R5: ρ=1.0\rho=1.0) are empirically verifiable and conceptually independent of the very calibration target the cohort design has shown to be unfit. This is the precise sense in which we describe the contribution as an epistemological intervention rather than as an improved estimator of the prevailing target.

Theory–measurement alignment.

Theorem 1 establishes a bound on joint mutual information I⁡(E,Ot)I(E;O^{t}); SFS is the operational metric. The contribution is not only the bound but the empirical alignment between theoretical prediction and operational measurement, holding across 18,430 successful trials, 16 conditions, and two cross-architecture models—to our knowledge the first such bridging in the multi-agent reasoning literature, where prior work reports either MI-style bounds without operational instantiation (Choi et al., 2025a) or operational metrics without information-theoretic grounding (Min et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2024). The per-round trajectories (Appendix B.3, Figure 7) directly visualise the alignment: F⁡(t)F(t) declines monotonically across rounds in C4 SocraSynth on both GPT-4o (0.156 round 1 →\to 0.125 round 4) and Claude-3.5-Sonnet (0.172 round 1 →\to 0.133 round 3), with cross-model Spearman ρ=0.94\rho=0.94 on trajectory shape—empirical confirmation that the directionality predicted by the bound holds at the level of individual debate rounds, not just aggregate condition means.

A fundamental limit on closed-system parametric reasoning.

The bound is more than a diagnosis of MAD: it identifies a ceiling that any closed-system parametric reasoning protocol satisfying the four conditions of Theorem 1 must obey—when the only information about EE at round t+1t{+}1 is what survived round tt, expected faithfulness cannot be regenerated from within the chain. The four formal results of §3—Theorem 1, Theorem 2, Lemma 2, and Proposition 1—together yield a tractable classification: closed-system protocols are bounded above (the Reasoning Trap regime), open-system protocols re-injecting EE are bounded below (the recovery regime), and vote-aggregating protocols collapse to the KK-way information floor regardless of chain length. Five paradigms inherit the closed-system ceiling (MAD, single-agent CoT, Reflexion, linear ToT, the broader token-Markov class); two principled exclusions (Self-Consistency, MoE) escape only by violating the Markov closure the bound presupposes. Read through the information bottleneck lens (Tishby et al., 2000), closed-system reasoning compresses representations of EE at each aggregation step in a manner no internal mechanism can reverse—only external evidence re-injection (Corollary 1, Appendix C.7) restores the lost information. The recovery side is what Theorem 2 formalises (sub-martingale property under external evidence re-injection), with Lemma 2 discharging the application to EGSR.

Implications and limitations.

Brown-Cohen et al. (2023), Buhl and others (2025), and Lang and others (2025) build safety arguments on the premise that debate’s accuracy convergence entails faithfulness convergence; the DPI bound provides a counter-premise: in the closed-system regime the bound covers, the expected joint MI cannot increase along the chain, with strict inequality whenever round-aggregation is non-injective (e.g., majority voting). Systems evaluated solely on accuracy may reward architectures producing polished but decreasingly faithful reasoning. We recommend faithfulness reporting alongside accuracy and explicit specification of whether the debate protocol satisfies or violates Theorem 1’s closed-system conditions. The recommendation is concrete: each protocol should declare which of the four conditions (shared θ\theta, EE provided once at t=0t{=}0, step t+1t{+}1 depends only on step tt output, symmetric aggregation) it satisfies or violates, and faithfulness claims should be conditioned on that declaration.

Limitations. EGSR is a process-faithfulness protocol, not an answer-maximisation protocol. H10 fails: C12 (EGSR+SLM) accuracy is 14% below the C1 baseline on out-of-distribution scientific claims while SFS recovers to 0.338 (97% of baseline). For applications where final answer accuracy is the optimisation target, EGSR is not the right tool; for applications where the reasoning trace must be defensible against external evidence, it is. Two further conditional limits: EGSR’s faithfulness is conditional on the quality of EE (C14: 5.5% SFS degradation under adversarial evidence injection)—if the externally injected evidence is itself unreliable, the recovery is partial. SFS’s decomposer is LLM-dependent (GPT-4o for primary results, Claude-3.5-Sonnet for cross-decomposer robustness in R4); R4–R5 show condition-level rankings are decomposer-invariant (ρ=1.0\rho=1.0), but the decomposition pipeline is not yet model-free. Full limitation discussion: Appendix C.

Toward AI that can think differently.

The Reasoning Trap may be read as a symptom of a deeper limit: autoregressive next-token predictors do not reliably produce the cognitive reframing faithful reasoning sometimes demands. Duncker (1945)’s candle problem and Wertheimer (1959)’s productive thinking name the demand; Boden (2004)’s transformational creativity is what closed-system reasoning chains, under the conditions of Theorem 1, do not appear to generate from within (Fauconnier and Turner, 2002; Gentner, 1983; Kuhn, 1962; Karmiloff-Smith, 1992). Copies from the same distribution may not introduce epistemic novelty: Surowiecki (2004)’s three conditions (diversity, independence, decentralization) and Hong and Page (2004)’s diversity-prediction theorem identify independence as a condition standard MAD does not satisfy (Wang and others, 2024); Polanyi (1966)’s “we can know more than we can tell” implies token-level outputs carry only the explicit residue of meaning. Recent work shows the best human divergent thinkers still outperform frontier LLMs even where group means converge (Koivisto and Grassini, 2023; Hubert et al., 2024; Bellemare-Pepin et al., 2024). EGSR’s effect appears to derive not from making models think differently but from supplying—from outside the model’s distribution—structured questions and external evidence the model does not generate on its own. Whether AI can be made to think differently (in Boden’s transformational sense) within the same parametric family remains an open question this paper deliberately does not foreclose; what we establish is the negative half: closed-system iteration cannot do it on its own.

8 Conclusion

Multi-agent debate tends to preserve answer accuracy while leaving unmodeled the information-theoretic chain through which evidence becomes claim—a gap associated with measurable faithfulness degradation. We call this the Debate Trap and offer a diagnostic metric (SFS), a remedial protocol (EGSR), and a theoretical bound 𝔼⁡[I⁡(E,Ot+1)]≤𝔼⁡[I⁡(E,Ot)]\mathbb{E}[I(E;O^{t+1})]\leq\mathbb{E}[I(E;O^{t})] along any Markov chain E→O0→O1→⋯E\to O^{0}\to O^{1}\to\cdots (Theorem 1). Across 18,430 successful trials (16 conditions on SciFact and FEVER), two architectures, and a triple-failure human evaluation across two language-and-domain cohorts, the Trap-proper configuration (DebateCV) preserves 88% of baseline accuracy while SFS drops 43%, majority-vote MAD reduces SFS to 1.7%, and EGSR recovers 98%. R6 adds a second visibility: the two cross-cohort raters applying the same rubric in a different language shift their own Q1Q_{1} means by 0.8–1.4 Likert points and Q2Q_{2} rates by 28–47 pp; metrics calibrated against decomposer-invariant rankings (R4–R5) do not inherit this instability.

A partition of multi-step LLM reasoning.

Theorem 1 (closed-system DPI ceiling), Theorem 2 (open-system faithfulness recovery), Lemma 2 (EGSR information accumulation), and Proposition 1 (vote-aggregation floor) together partition multi-step LLM reasoning protocols by their information-theoretic relationship to EE: closed-system protocols cannot regenerate I⁡(E,Ot)I(E;O^{t}) internally; open-system protocols re-injecting EE form sub-martingales; vote-aggregating protocols collapse to the KK-way information floor. The partition explains the three observed tiers (§6) and the C15 floor as structural predictions, reproduced on Claude-3.5-Sonnet and FEVER rather than being GPT-4o-specific. The contribution is the closure: formal results sufficient to classify any candidate protocol before empirical testing.

Implications for evaluation practice.

Three recommendations follow: (i) report faithfulness alongside accuracy on multi-agent benchmarks, since accuracy alone can reward decreasingly grounded reasoning; (ii) each protocol should declare whether it satisfies or violates Theorem 1’s closed-system + shared-θ\theta + symmetric-aggregation conditions; (iii) scalable-oversight proposals built on the convergence assumption (Brown-Cohen et al., 2023; Buhl and others, 2025; Lang and others, 2025) deserve a faithfulness-grounded re-evaluation in light of Theorem 1.

Falsifiable forecast.

We close with one conjecture, framed as a research program rather than a tested claim: any closed-system reasoning protocol preserving the Markov structure of Theorem 1 is, in expectation, bounded by the DPI. The implication is not that CoT, ToT, or Reflexion necessarily fail, but that closed-system variants may share this structural vulnerability unless evidence is reintroduced; cross-paradigm validation—Self-Consistency and MoE excluded—is the natural next step. The bound is a candidate ceiling rather than a contingent architectural feature. We hope this contributes to a shift in multi-agent evaluation practice from “does the answer improve?” to “does the reasoning remain grounded in the evidence?”
