Acknowledgments

The author is deeply grateful to the eleven R6 cohort raters who undertook the reasoning-faithfulness evaluation. The task was unusually demanding: each item required reading a multi-step LLM reasoning trace alongside its evidence corpus, decomposing the reasoning into atomic claims, and assigning Likert-5 faithfulness scores together with binary unsupported-claim flags—under a rubric calibrated against Landis and Koch (1977)’s interpretation table. The Korean cohort (R1–R8 plus the cross-cohort raters R-H and R-L) evaluated 3030 FEVER items each (300300 ratings total); the English cohort (R-H, R-L, and R-K) evaluated 200200 SciFact items each; the two cross-cohort raters (R-H and R-L) voluntarily completed both cohorts, providing the cross-language intra-rater test-retest data from which the R6 triple-failure result is derived. Without their patience and careful judgement, the central empirical finding of this paper—that the human signal against which faithfulness metrics have been calibrated is not itself a stable measurement target under prevailing rater-calibration practices—would not have been observable. To preserve participant confidentiality consistent with the cohort-design protocol, raters are referenced throughout this paper by their anonymisation codes only (R1–R8 for the eight Korean-cohort-only raters, R-H and R-L for the two cross-cohort raters, and R-K for the English-cohort-only rater).

The author also acknowledges the broader methodological tradition in faithfulness research (Maynez et al., 2020; Honovich et al., 2022; Min et al., 2023; Jacovi and Goldberg, 2020) that this paper builds upon and respectfully extends.

Appendix A Knowledge Frontier Map of Reasoning Faithfulness Research

This appendix expands on §2. We first present the lineage map (Figure 5), then summarize the eight active lineages in detail (one paragraph per lineage); finally we catalogue the 89 most central of 132 contributions in Table 2, annotated by core claim, boundary, and relation to the present work.

A.1 Eight Lineages on Multi-Agent Reasoning Faithfulness

(L1) CoT faithfulness in single agents. Turpin et al. [2023] demonstrated that chain-of-thought explanations are post-hoc rationalizations; subsequent work refined the claim through causal mediation [Paul et al., 2024], scalability paradoxes [Shen et al., 2026, Tanneru et al., 2024], decoupling probes [Jiang and others, 2025], causal-concept analysis [Matton and others, 2025], and streaming detection [Lu and others, 2026, Mittal and Arike, 2026, Cheng and others, 2025]. None addresses multi-agent settings.

(L2) MAD critique. Du et al. [2023] introduced MAD as an accuracy-improvement tool. Subsequent evaluations report that MAD does not consistently beat self-consistency [Wang et al., 2023, Zhang et al., 2025, Yang et al., 2025] and that majority voting matches the best MAD configuration [Choi et al., 2025a, Kenton et al., 2024, Rahman and others, 2025]. Failure mechanisms include problem drift [Becker et al., 2025], sycophancy [Pitre et al., 2025, Yao and others, 2025], identity bias [Choi et al., 2025b], and structural inability to genuinely debate [Wu et al., 2025, Tang and others, 2025, Wynn and others, 2025, Han and others, 2025, Kim and others, 2024, Koupaee and others, 2025]. Mitigations target accuracy: peer-prediction weighting [Liu et al., 2026], confidence calibration [Zhu and others, 2026], model heterogeneity [Chang, 2024]. None measures faithfulness directly.

(L3) Faithfulness/factuality metrics. FActScore [Min et al., 2023], SAFE [Wei et al., 2024], VeriScore [Song et al., 2024], DnDScore [Wanner and others, 2024], FactTest [Nie and others, 2024], VeriFastScore [Rajendhran and others, 2025], OpenFActScore [Lage and others, 2025], and HalluMeasure [Akbar and others, 2024] measure factual precision in single-agent generation. None tracks faithfulness across debate rounds; none verifies against the specific evidence set provided to a multi-agent system.

(L4) Sycophancy and convergence. Sharma et al. [2024] showed that RLHF preference data systematically reward agreement (“matches user’s beliefs” is the strongest single predictor); Perez and others [2022] discovered the behaviour; Chen and others [2024] localized it to ∼\sim4% of attention heads; Kim and Khashabi [2025] showed that conversational framing amplifies sycophancy 3.4×\times over evaluative framing. Constitutional AI [Bai and others, 2022] and pinpoint tuning [Chen and others, 2024] mitigate at the user-facing level; none addresses agent-agent dynamics.

(L5) Accuracy–faithfulness divergence. Nguyen and others [2024] report that knowledge-graph evaluation reveals accuracy-faithfulness decoupling; Jacovi and Goldberg [2020] formalised the conceptual distinction; DeYoung et al. [2020] provided an early benchmark. We extend the divergence into the multi-agent setting.

(L6) AI safety via debate. Irving et al. [2018] originated the program; Brown-Cohen et al. [2023] provided the doubly-efficient theoretical extension; Lang and others [2025] applied it to weak-to-strong generalization; Buhl and others [2025] and Arnesen et al. [2024] examined empirical limitations. The lineage assumes that convergence toward correct answers entails convergence toward faithful reasoning.

(L7) Socratic reasoning as alternative. Qi and others [2023], He et al. [2024], Kumar and Lan [2024], Shi and others [2025], Miao and others [2024], Kargupta et al. [2024] replace adversarial debate with structured questioning; all operate within the model’s own knowledge. EGSR adds external evidence as the verification anchor.

(L8) Metacognition and self-reflection. Shinn and others [2023], Bai and others [2022], Guo and others [2025], Yu and others [2025], Walker and others [2025], Shukla and others (NVIDIA) [2025], Yang and others (SJTU+OPPO) [2024], Li et al. [2024] attempt internal self-correction; Hubinger and others [2024] caution that adversarial training hides rather than removes deception, a failure mode that Guo [2024] maps in greater detail.

B.3 Cross-Model Replication and Faithfulness Trajectory

Claude-3.5-Sonnet replicates the C15 SFS collapse (SFS = 0.011, 3.2% of baseline) and the EGSR recovery (SFS = 0.331, 95% of baseline). Cross-model condition rankings preserve the SciFact orderings (Spearman ρ=0.94\rho=0.94). The Debate Trap is not specific to GPT-4o.

Per-round faithfulness trajectory.

For C4 (SocraSynth, 5 rounds), GPT-4o shows a clear decline: mean SFS drops from 0.1560.156 at round 1 to 0.1250.125 at round 4—a 20% degradation within the debate—before partially recovering to 0.1310.131 at round 5. The sharpest drop occurs between rounds 1 and 2 (Δ=−0.024\Delta=-0.024), consistent with the first exchange of arguments triggering rapid conformity. Claude-3.5-Sonnet on the same condition shows the same pattern: SFS falls from 0.1720.172 (round 1) to 0.1330.133 (round 3), with cross-model Spearman ρ=0.94\rho=0.94 on the per-round trajectory. These trajectories empirically confirm Theorem 1’s prediction that faithfulness is non-increasing under standard MAD: the aggregate trend is downward, even though individual rounds may fluctuate. Figure 7 visualizes both C4 (debate, decreasing) and C8 (EGSR, sub-martingale increasing) trajectories on both models.

B.4 R6 Pairwise Cohen’s κ\kappa Matrix

Figure 8 reports the pairwise Cohen’s κ\kappa on the binary Q2Q_{2} “unsupported claim” flag across all 11 raters in the R6 cohorts. The maximum pair κ=+0.583\kappa=+0.583 (Rater L vs. Rater K, the only cross-cohort pair) does not reach Substantial agreement. B.7 LLM-as-auditor Probe (Empirical)

We probed Theorem 1’s implication empirically by re-evaluating the Q1 dataset of §6.2 with six frontier LLMs as zero-shot auditors: GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Llama-3-70B, Mistral-Small-24B (via OpenRouter), and Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct-Turbo (via Together AI free-tier). Of 15 R6 records, the human cohort scored 0/15 in identifying unfaithful debate reasoning; LLM auditors averaged 6/15 (40%, max 9/15 = 60% for Llama-3-70B). The 6×\times improvement of LLM-as-auditor over human-as-auditor on the same items suggests that automated faithfulness measurement may serve as a complementary signal rather than a mere substitute for unstable humans.

Appendix C Extended Discussion

C.1 Conditions Specification

The 16 experimental conditions span four families. Baselines (C1 zero-shot, C2 RAG, C3 SocCoT). Debate (C4 SocraSynth, C6 Debate+RAG, C13 DebateCV, C15 Vanilla MAD, C16 UDPO). EGSR variants (C8 core, C9 Parallel, C12 +SLM, C14 +Adversarial). Competitors and ablations (C5 SocraticNet, C7 Pipeline-noSLM, C10 Internal Socratic, C11 SSR [Shi and others, 2025]). Per-condition prompts, agent counts, round limits, and aggregation rules are reproduced verbatim in the supplementary materials and the GitHub repository.

C.2 Robustness Experiment Protocols (R1–R8)

R1 (Similarity).

Three similarity functions: word overlap (Jaccard on token sets), sentence-BERT (all-MiniLM-L6-v2), and DeBERTa-v3-large NLI entailment. 200 claims ×\times 8 conditions per function.

R3 (Threshold sensitivity).

NLI threshold τ∈{0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9}\tau\in\{0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9\}. Condition rankings preserved across all τ\tau; absolute SFS values shift by ≤0.05\leq 0.05.

R4 (Decomposer reliability).

GPT-4o vs. Claude-3.5-Sonnet as decomposers on 150 reasoning texts (50 per condition for C1, C4, C8). Mean soft-Jaccard 0.49; condition rankings perfectly preserved (Spearman ρ=1.0\rho=1.0); per-text claim counts correlate at ρ=0.57\rho=0.57, p<10−14p<10^{-14}.

R5 (Cross-decomposer agreement).

75% of decomposition pairs achieve soft-Jaccard ≥0.30\geq 0.30; 49% exceed 0.500.50.

R2 (Verbosity control, post-hoc).

Across all 13,630 successful FEVER evaluations, the Pearson correlation between reasoning length (characters) and SFS is r=−0.0245r=-0.0245 (Spearman ρ=+0.054\rho=+0.054): essentially zero. SFS does not reward verbose outputs, ruling out length as a confounder of the SFS conclusions.

R6 (Human evaluation).

Detailed protocol, rubric, and per-rater outputs in Appendix B.8 above. Two language-and-domain cohorts; Fleiss κ\kappa at most +0.018+0.018 for Likert-5; intra-rater Q1 shifts −0.80-0.80 and +1.40+1.40 across language.

R8 (FActScore comparison).

SFS and FActScore correlate at r=0.61r=0.61; FActScore ranks debate higher than EGSR (C4 = 0.59, C1 = 0.32) due to fluency confound.

C.3 Detailed Limitations

Knowledge gap.

EGSR cannot supply knowledge the model does not have. H10’s failure (C12 accuracy 14% below baseline on out-of-distribution scientific claims) shows that SFS guarantees faithfulness, not correctness. Retrieval augmentation that feeds external evidence into EGSR’s verification step (rather than into the reasoning step) is the natural complement; we leave its implementation to future work.

Evidence quality.

EGSR’s faithfulness guarantees are conditional on the quality of the evidence set EE. C14 (EGSR + Adversarial Evidence) shows partial robustness: SFS drops from 0.343 to 0.324 (5.5%), not to zero. The threshold at which adversarial evidence breaks EGSR remains an open empirical question.

Decomposition dependence.

SFS relies on a language model for atomic decomposition. R4–R5 show condition-level rankings preserved across decomposer choice (Spearman ρ=1.0\rho=1.0), but absolute SFS values may shift. We mitigate verification via DeBERTa-v3 NLI rather than LLM-based judgement, but the decomposition step remains LLM-dependent. The scalability paradox of Shen et al. [2026]—that stronger models produce harder-to-detect unfaithfulness—may apply to the decomposition step itself.

FEVER replication of EGSR.

The full-scale FEVER replication confirms the Debate Trap (H1, H7, C15/C16 collapse), but does not reproduce the EGSR-vs-baseline contrasts H4–H6 from SciFact. The reason is methodological: in our SciFact analysis, EGSR retrieves passages from the SciFact abstract corpus at inference time, whereas the FEVER replication’s EGSR variant generates its evidence pool with the same model that produces the reasoning, to match the cost profile of the other 12 conditions. The FEVER EGSR result is closer to “Socratic self-questioning with self-generated evidence” than to the original protocol. This limitation does not affect the C15/C16 collapse, which is a property of vote-aggregating reasoning regardless of evidence source.

C.4 Extended Sycophancy Mechanism

The three-level sycophancy model (training, architectural, contextual) discussed in §2 is partially testable in our experimental design. At the training level, both GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet exhibit the C15 collapse, consistent with RLHF-induced sycophancy persisting across model providers [Sharma et al., 2024]. At the contextual level, the gap between C10 (Internal Socratic, SFS = 0.308) and C8 (EGSR, SFS = 0.343) shows that evaluative framing (EGSR’s hypothesis-free verification) outperforms conversational framing (Internal Socratic’s self-questioning), consistent with Kim and Khashabi’s finding that evaluative framing reduces sycophancy. The architectural level remains untested; probing whether debate specifically activates the ∼\sim4% sycophancy heads identified by Chen and others [2024] is a promising direction for future work.

C.5 SFS Axioms (A1–A7)

A1 (Granularity). SFS operates at claim level, not response level.
A2 (Decomposer-invariant rankings). Condition orderings preserved across decomposers (R4–R5 verify).
A3 (Evidence-set sensitivity). SFS depends on the specific EE provided; identical reasoning can yield different SFS under different EE.
A4 (Support-mass monotonicity). Adding an entailed claim weakly increases the total support mass ∑isi\sum_{i}s_{i}. Since SFS⁡(O)=1N​∑isi\mathrm{SFS}(O)=\tfrac{1}{N}\sum_{i}s_{i} is the support-mass average, adding a claim with support below the current average lowers the average even when the addition is well-supported; we therefore report average SFS together with claim count, EUR, and unsupported-claim diagnostics so that average movements are interpretable in context.
A5 (Fabrication penalty). Adding an unsupported claim (si=0s_{i}=0) weakly decreases average SFS whenever the current average is non-negative, and strictly decreases it when SFS⁡(O)>0\mathrm{SFS}(O)>0: unsupported claims contribute zero to the numerator while still incrementing the denominator.
A6 (Reproducibility). Full pipeline open-sourced; deterministic given seed.
A7 (Same verdict, different SFS). Two outputs with identical verdicts can have different SFS values reflecting reasoning-process differences (R7 verifies).

C.6 EGSR Algorithm Specification

Figure 9 contrasts the information-flow structure of the two regimes: closed-system MAD (Theorem 1, F⁡(t)F(t) non-increasing) vs. open-system EGSR (Theorem 2, sub-martingale F⁡(t)↑F(t)\uparrow). The architectural realization of the open-system regime is shown in Figure 10.

EGSR proceeds in up to K=3K=3 iterations. Each iteration generates one Socratic question (cycling through six predefined types: clarification, assumption-probing, evidence-demanding, counter-example-seeking, implication-exploring, meta-evaluation), retrieves the top-5 evidence passages, checks evidence sufficiency (ESS), and verifies the answer via Hypothesis-Free Socratic Verification (HFSV)—answering using only the retrieved passages, without access to the original claim text or prior reasoning. The verdict aggregator updates after each iteration; convergence is declared when 2-of-3 criteria are met (ESS ≥0.75\geq 0.75, stable verdict, confidence gap >0.20>0.20). Empirically, 90% of EGSR evaluations converge in a single iteration, indicating that the evidence-grounding step is typically sufficient on the first pass.

C.7 Formal Companion Results to Theorem 1

The four results that together partition the space of multi-step LLM reasoning protocols by their information-theoretic relationship to EE are: Theorem 1 (closed-system upper bound, body), and the three companions below. Lemma 1 formalises the load-bearing quantity, Theorem 2 states the open-system recovery counterpart, Lemma 2 applies it to EGSR, and Proposition 1 states the vote-aggregation floor.

Lemma 1 (Joint-MI as the Canonical Faithfulness Quantity under Symmetry).

Under symmetric agents (identical θ\theta), the joint-MI faithfulness Fjoint​(t):=I⁡(E,Ot)F^{\mathrm{joint}}(t):=I(E;O^{t}) is the natural information-theoretic quantity to which the Data Processing Inequality directly applies (Theorem 1). The per-agent average F⁡(t)=1n​∑iFi​(t)F(t)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}F_{i}(t) provides a complementary symmetry-respecting summary; the two are not identical in general (redundant information across agents implies Fjoint≠1n​∑iFiF^{\mathrm{joint}}\neq\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}F_{i} outside trivial cases). We use FjointF^{\mathrm{joint}} as the load-bearing object.

Corollary 1 (EGSR breaks the Markov chain).

If the reasoning protocol re-accesses the evidence EE at each round tt, the Markov property Ot+1⟂E|OtO^{t+1}\perp E\mid O^{t} no longer holds. The dependency structure becomes Ot+1=g⁡(Ot,E,Qt)O^{t+1}=g(O^{t},E,Q^{t}) where QtQ^{t} are queries generated at round tt; I⁡(E,Ot+1)I(E;O^{t+1}) is no longer bounded above by I⁡(E,Ot)I(E;O^{t}).

Theorem 2 (Faithfulness Recovery under Open-System Information Accumulation).

Suppose at each round t+1t{+}1, the reasoning protocol produces Ot+1=(Ot,At+1)O^{t+1}=(O^{t},A^{t+1}) where At+1A^{t+1} is auxiliary information generated with direct access to EE (e.g., retrieved passages, verified atomic claims, evidence-grounded Socratic answers). Then I⁡(E,Ot+1)≥I⁡(E,Ot)I(E;O^{t+1})\geq I(E;O^{t}), and F⁡(t)F(t) is a sub-martingale: 𝔼⁡[F⁡(t+1)∣F⁡(t)]≥F⁡(t)\mathbb{E}[F(t+1)\mid F(t)]\geq F(t). The inequality is strict whenever At+1A^{t+1} carries information about EE not already contained in OtO^{t}.

Lemma 2 (EGSR is information-accumulating).

Under EGSR’s running-aggregate verdict update (Appendix C.6), the round-t+1t{+}1 output OEGSRt+1O^{t+1}_{\mathrm{EGSR}} contains OEGSRtO^{t}_{\mathrm{EGSR}} as a sub-component, augmented by externally retrieved evidence and a verifier-gated atomic claim. Theorem 2 therefore applies: EGSR is a sub-martingale for faithfulness.

Proposition 1 (Vote-Aggregation Floor).

Let VKV_{K} denote a verdict space of size KK. Under any protocol whose final output strips atomic claims and reduces OTO^{T} to a vote tally v∈VKv\in V_{K}, the operational faithfulness satisfies SFS⁡(OT)→0\mathrm{SFS}(O^{T})\to 0 as the vote tally contains no atomic claims to verify against EE. Equivalently, I⁡(E,OT)≤H⁡(v)≤log2⁡KI(E;O^{T})\leq H(v)\leq\log_{2}K regardless of H⁡(E)H(E), and the SFS-realized bound collapses to zero when no decomposable claims remain. C15’s empirical 0.0060.006 floor (1.7% of baseline) instantiates this prediction.

C.8 Proof Sketches for Formal Results

Proof sketch of Lemma 1 (Joint-MI as Canonical Quantity).

Under symmetric agents (identical parameters θ\theta), I⁡(E,Oit)=I⁡(E,Ojt)I(E;O_{i}^{t})=I(E;O_{j}^{t}) for all i,ji,j by symmetry, so the per-agent average 1n​∑iFi​(t)=Fi​(t)\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}F_{i}(t)=F_{i}(t) for any single ii. The joint quantity Fjoint​(t)=I⁡(E,Ot)F^{\mathrm{joint}}(t)=I(E;O^{t}) is the natural object to which DPI applies along the Markov chain E→O0→O1→⋯E\to O^{0}\to O^{1}\to\cdots, and we use it as the load-bearing quantity in Theorem 1. We do not claim Fjoint​(t)=1n​∑iFi​(t)F^{\mathrm{joint}}(t)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}F_{i}(t) in general: redundant information across agents (a typical feature of debate among copies of the same model) implies Fjoint≠1n​∑iFiF^{\mathrm{joint}}\neq\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}F_{i} outside trivial cases. The two are complementary symmetry-respecting summaries of the same multi-agent information state; the per-agent average F⁡(t)F(t) remains useful for inspecting individual-agent behaviour, but the bound in Theorem 1 is stated in terms of FjointF^{\mathrm{joint}}.∎

Proof of Theorem 1 (DPI Bound).

Under standard MAD, agent ii’s output at round t+1t+1 is a deterministic (or stochastic with shared randomness) function of the aggregate output at round tt and the shared parameters θ\theta. The information-theoretic chain E→O0→O1→⋯→OTE\to O^{0}\to O^{1}\to\cdots\to O^{T} is therefore a Markov chain conditioned on θ\theta. The Data Processing Inequality (DPI) yields I⁡(E,Ot+1)≤I⁡(E,Ot)I(E;O^{t+1})\leq I(E;O^{t}) for all tt. Taking expectations, 𝔼⁡[Fjoint​(t+1)]≤𝔼⁡[Fjoint​(t)]\mathbb{E}[F^{\mathrm{joint}}(t+1)]\leq\mathbb{E}[F^{\mathrm{joint}}(t)] where Fjoint​(t)=I⁡(E,Ot)F^{\mathrm{joint}}(t)=I(E;O^{t}) (Lemma 1). The inequality is strict whenever the round-t+1t+1 aggregation is non-injective in OtO^{t} (vote-aggregating, summary-aggregating, or majority-selecting protocols).∎

Proof of Theorem 2 (Faithfulness Recovery).

Given Ot+1=(Ot,At+1)O^{t+1}=(O^{t},A^{t+1}) where At+1A^{t+1} is auxiliary information with direct access to EE, mutual information is monotonic under the addition of variables: I⁡(E,(Ot,At+1))≥I⁡(E,Ot)I(E;(O^{t},A^{t+1}))\geq I(E;O^{t}). Hence I⁡(E,Ot+1)≥I⁡(E,Ot)I(E;O^{t+1})\geq I(E;O^{t}). The inequality is strict whenever At+1A^{t+1} carries information about EE not already contained in OtO^{t}, i.e., whenever I⁡(E;At+1∣Ot)>0I(E;A^{t+1}\mid O^{t})>0. Taking expectations, F⁡(t)F(t) is a sub-martingale.∎

Proof of Lemma 2 (EGSR Information Accumulation).

By the EGSR algorithm (Appendix C.6), at each iteration kk the verdict aggregator updates vkv_{k} based on (vk−1,ak,ESSk)(v_{k-1},a_{k},\text{ESS}_{k}), where aka_{k} is a verifier-gated answer to the Socratic question qkq_{k} retrieved against EE via Rk=Retrieve⁡(qk,E,top​-​5)R_{k}=\mathrm{Retrieve}(q_{k},E,\mathrm{top}\text{-}5). The output OEGSRkO^{k}_{\mathrm{EGSR}} thus contains OEGSRk−1O^{k-1}_{\mathrm{EGSR}} (running aggregate) augmented by Ak+1=(qk,Rk,ak)A^{k+1}=(q_{k},R_{k},a_{k}), all of which depend on EE via the Retrieve step. The conditions of Theorem 2 are satisfied.∎

Proof of Proposition 1 (Vote-Aggregation Floor).

For any random variable vv taking values in a discrete set of size KK, H⁡(v)≤log2⁡KH(v)\leq\log_{2}K with equality iff vv is uniformly distributed. Hence I⁡(E,v)≤min⁡(H⁡(E),H⁡(v))≤log2⁡KI(E;v)\leq\min(H(E),H(v))\leq\log_{2}K. The SFS proxy decomposes OTO^{T} into atomic claims {c1,…,cN}\{c_{1},\ldots,c_{N}\}; when OTO^{T} is a vote tally with no decomposable atomic content, N→0N\to 0 in the relevant subset and the operational SFS approaches zero. C15 (§6) instantiates this floor empirically: three-round majority voting strips the reasoning to a vote tally and SFS collapses to 0.0060.006.∎

Appendix D Visual Supplementary

This appendix collects eight visual summaries that complement the prose-based discussion in the main body and Appendices B–C. Each figure is designed as a stand-alone reference and answers a specific reviewer question without requiring re-reading of the main text.

D.1 A Map of Reasoning Faithfulness in the LLM Era (referenced from §2)

Figure 11 situates the present work within five generations of multi-step reasoning research. The single-agent stem evolves Gen I (outcome benchmarking, 1995–2020) →\rightarrow Gen II (self-rationalization with explicit Chain-of-Thought, 2020–2023) →\rightarrow Gen III (CoT faithfulness as a research target, 2023–2026); the multi-agent fork from Gen I gives rise to Gen IV (MAD descriptive analysis, 2023–2026); both streams converge into Generation V (the present work, 2026–), which integrates the metric (SFS), algorithm (EGSR), and theorem (DPI Bound) into a single package—none present in Generation III or IV individually. The four corner boxes (Q1–Q4) map directly to the paper’s four contributions.

D.2 Reliability of the Ground Truth Itself (referenced from §2)

Figure 12 positions the prior art on two axes—inter- vs. within-rater agreement (horizontal) and single- vs. cross-language/domain coverage (vertical)—and shows that the upper-right quadrant (cross-language within-rater test-retest of reasoning-faithfulness judgement) has remained empty across the 132 contributions catalogued in Appendix A.2. The R6 cohort design (§6.2) tests this directly via two raters who completed both Korean FEVER and English SciFact cohorts, finding intra-rater shifts of Δ​Q1∈{−0.80,+1.40}\Delta Q_{1}\in\{-0.80,+1.40\} Likert points and Δ​Q2∈{+28.0,−47.5}\Delta Q_{2}\in\{+28.0,-47.5\} percentage points across language and domain.

D.3 DPI Markov Chain (referenced from §3)

Figure 13 visualizes Theorem 1’s closed-system Markov chain. External evidence EE is provided once at t=0t{=}0 and the chain evolves under shared parameters θ\theta without re-injection; by the Data Processing Inequality, the joint mutual information I⁡(E,Ot)I(E;O^{t}) is non-increasing in expectation along the chain, strictly so whenever round-t+1t{+}1 aggregation is non-injective. EGSR breaks this chain by re-accessing EE at each verification step (Corollary 1), violating condition (ii) of the four-condition closure (Appendix D.5).

D.4 R6 Triple Failure of Human Reliability (referenced from §6)

Figure 14 reports the three-panel R6 result that motivates SFS’s framing as a decomposer-invariant operationalisation rather than an approximation to a human-calibrated target. Panel (a) shows inter-rater Fleiss κ\kappa at most +0.018+0.018 in either cohort; panel (b) shows the two raters who completed both cohorts shifted their Q1Q_{1} means in opposite directions; panel (c) shows only 4.5%4.5\% of 200 SciFact items achieved 3-rater unanimity while 25.0%25.0\% exhibited maximum-spread disagreement. Together the three panels document that the human signal, under rating practices prevalent in the faithfulness-metric literature, is not itself a stable measurement target.

D.5 Generalization of Theorem 1: Five Paradigms In Scope, Two Outside

Theorem 1’s closed-system bound applies to any reasoning protocol satisfying the four conditions (i)–(iv) introduced in §3. Figure 15 verifies the conditions across five paradigms within scope (multi-agent debate, single-agent CoT, Reflexion, linear-traversal Tree-of-Thought, and the broader token-Markov class) and two principled exclusions (Self-Consistency and Mixture-of-Experts). The grid shows at a glance that the bound is not specific to MAD; it is a property of any reasoning protocol that satisfies the closed-system + shared-θ\theta + symmetric-aggregation requirements.

D.6 Cost-Faithfulness Pareto Frontier

Figure 16 positions all 16 SciFact conditions in the cost-faithfulness plane (development-time API cost in $ per claim, log scale, vs. SFS). The Pareto-optimal region (low cost, high SFS) is the upper-left corner. EGSR variants (C8, C9, C12, C14) cluster in this region with pipeline-level cost (∼\sim$0.05/claim) and near-baseline SFS (∼\sim0.34). Debate variants (C4, C6, C13) occupy the dominated region (high cost, low SFS); C15 and C16 reach the lower band (SFS →0\to 0). The dashed Pareto frontier connects EGSR (C8) and the zero-shot baseline (C1)—no condition outperforms both simultaneously.

D.7 Pre-registered Hypothesis Tests with Holm-Bonferroni Correction

Figure 17 reports the pre-registered hypothesis tests with effect sizes (Cohen’s dd) and 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The eight-test primary family (H1, H2, H4–H9) is corrected under Holm-Bonferroni at α=0.05\alpha=0.05 (adjusted threshold α∗=0.0100\alpha^{*}=0.0100); seven of the eight pass with p<10−2p<10^{-2}, and H7 (Parallel ≥\geq Sequential) is marginal (p=0.43p=0.43, d=−0.02d=-0.02). H3 was originally pre-registered as “SFS-human correlation r>0.70r>0.70” but rendered inconclusive by the R6 finding that the human signal, under prevailing rater-calibration practices, is not a stable measurement target (§6.2); it is reported descriptively. H10 (SLM accuracy parity) is also reported descriptively as a secondary observation.

D.8 Sycophancy as a Three-Level Cascade

The sycophancy mechanism discussed in §7 operates at three levels in the LLM (training, architecture, context), each with a documented human-deliberation parallel (cultural socialization, groupthink symptoms, group polarization law). Figure 18 visualizes the cascade. EGSR’s external evidence anchor breaks the third level (Context): the conversational framing of MAD that amplifies sycophancy by 3.4×3.4\times [Kim and Khashabi, 2025] is replaced with evaluative framing in EGSR, in which the Checker verifies each atomic claim against EE rather than agreeing with peer agents.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
